Final exam characteristics The activities related to preparing the final exam for the Master's Degree in Biology are carried out by the student under the supervision of one or more tutor professors in the form of an internship at a university laboratory or a public or private external entity contracted with the University.
The objective of the internship is for the student to acquire in-depth knowledge of experimental methodology, analytical tools, and techniques for data analysis and processing.
The final exam requires the presentation of an experimental thesis summarizing the student's experience during the internship period, developed in an original manner under the guidance of the supervisor. The final objective is to present, discuss, and share acquired knowledge critically. The examining committee, based on results achieved during the study career and the quality of the thesis and its presentation, assigns a score out of 110.
Required knowledge for entry Students intending to enroll in the Master's Degree in Biology must hold a Master's degree or a three-year university diploma, or another foreign degree recognized as equivalent. They must possess, in addition to curricular requirements, adequate preparation in fundamental subjects for the profession of Biologist, such as Mathematics, Physics, Chemistry, and Computer Science, as well as in basic biological disciplines providing indispensable knowledge of living organisms at morphological, functional, and structural levels.
They must also possess knowledge of biochemical, molecular, and cellular mechanisms regulating inheritance, reproduction, and development. In particular, they must document prior acquisition of sufficient knowledge in the following core disciplines of the Master's Degree Program: Botany, Zoology, Ecology, Biochemistry, Molecular Biology, Cytology, Histology, Developmental Biology, Anatomy, Pathology, Microbiology, Hygiene, Physiology, Genetics, and Pharmacology.
1.
For admission to the Master's Degree in Biology, the following combined curricular requirements are mandatory:
i) holding a degree in one of the following classes under D.M. 270/04: L-13 Biological Sciences, L-2 Biotechnology, L-32 Environmental and Natural Sciences, LM-13 Pharmacy and Industrial Pharmacy; or in the following classes under D.M. 509/99: 12 Biological Sciences, 1 Biotechnology, 27 Environmental and Natural Sciences, 14-S Pharmacy and Industrial Pharmacy; alternatively, holding a degree under the previous D.M. 509/99 system (five-year degrees in Biological Sciences);
ii) having acquired at least 40 CFU in the SSDs BIO/01, BIO/05, BIO/06, BIO/07, BIO/09, BIO/10, BIO/11, BIO/12, BIO/13, BIO/14, BIO/16, BIO/18, BIO/19, MED/04, MED/07, MED/42.
2.
Graduates holding a degree different from those listed above must have acquired at least 75 CFU in the SSDs BIO/01, BIO/05, BIO/06, BIO/07, BIO/09, BIO/10, BIO/11, BIO/12, BIO/13, BIO/14, BIO/15, BIO/18, BIO/19, MED/04, MED/07, MED/42.
3.
For graduates from foreign universities, the adequacy of curricular requirements is assessed on a case-by-case basis based on the coherence between programs in different disciplinary areas, the foundational knowledge deemed necessary for the advanced training offered by the study program, and language skills.
For enrollment in the Master's Degree in Biology, knowledge of English in written and oral form at B1 level is required.
The verification of personal preparation, accessible only to those meeting curricular requirements, occurs through the modalities specified in the study program's teaching regulations.
Specific learning objectives.
The Master's Degree in Biology aims to train graduates with biomedical/pharmacological, physiological, biochemical, and naturalistic competencies, differently tailored according to application areas represented by two curriculum areas:
1. cellular-molecular;
2. nutritional.
Additionally, the training path is completed by Contextual Knowledge and Final Exam.
- CELLULAR-MOLECULAR AREA Includes courses relevant for acquiring knowledge and skills in cellular and biomolecular fields, both basic and applied, in areas such as biomolecule chemistry in -omics sciences (CHIM/06, BIO/10), cellular and molecular biology, and biodiversity in human, animal, and plant contexts (BIO/01-03, BIO/05-07, BIO/11, BIO/18), and biomedical microbiology (BIO/19, MED/07, MED/42). It also includes courses in areas such as physiology (BIO/09) and pharmacology and toxicology (BIO/14), both basic and applied.
- NUTRITIONAL AREA Includes courses relevant for acquiring knowledge and skills in nutritional fields, both basic and applied, in areas such as food chemistry and biochemistry (CHIM/06, CHIM/10, BIO/10), applied molecular biology in nutrigenetic and nutrigenomic contexts (BIO/11, BIO/18), pharmacology and nutraceutical principles (BIO/14), biodiversity, environmental sustainability, microbiology, hygiene, and food quality (BIO/01, BIO/03, BIO/05, BIO/19, MED/07, MED/42, AGR/15), applied physiology (BIO/09, MED/49), and pathophysiology (MED/04).
- CONTEXTUAL KNOWLEDGE AND FINAL EXAM Contextual knowledge completes the training of the Biologist and is achieved through:
a. laboratory experimental activities and exercises;
b. collection and processing of experimental data;
c. learning English at B2 level for communication and understanding of scientific publications, documents, and European regulations.
The conclusion of the training path above requires a final exam based on the work carried out by the student during the internship period, related to various aspects of biology, presented in a thesis following internationally accepted scientific standards.
Degree awarded.
Master's Degree III - Independent judgment The graduate acquires conscious independent judgment through the broad knowledge gained in core and/or professional disciplines, combined with internship activities (experimental and training) and/or internships in university, company, or public/private entity laboratories. Specifically, the graduate develops independent judgment regarding: i) project, structure, and personnel responsibility; ii) identification of new development perspectives and strategies; iii) evaluation, interpretation, and re-elaboration of literature data; iv) critical and responsible approach to ethical and bioethical issues.
Verification of achieving adequate independent judgment occurs through oral and/or written exams for each course. Additionally, the acquisition of independent judgment by the student is verified through journal club activities and during the final exam.
Knowledge and understanding.
generic area Master's graduates who successfully complete the program must have acquired the ability to understand and explain biological phenomena at chemical, biochemical, molecular, cellular, physiological-functional, anatomical, pathological, pharmacological, and population levels.
These knowledge and understanding capabilities are acquired and verified primarily through specific courses and competence-based exams of the respective curricula.
Ability to apply knowledge and understanding.
generic area Master's graduates who successfully complete the program must: a. possess skills in chemical and biochemical methodologies, biomolecular and bioinformatics methodologies, statistics, and data analysis for multidisciplinary application;
b. possess skills in study and understanding methods in various biological contexts;
c. have fully mastered the scientific method of investigation.
These skills are acquired using textbooks and articles with both theoretical and experimental content, as well as proposing exercises on current and concrete cases.
Particular emphasis is also placed on verifying these skills during the final exam evaluation.
IV - Communication skills The graduate acquires adequate communication skills and tools, referring to their ability to: i) present fluently in English using disciplinary terminology; ii) develop and present research and development projects; iii) organize group work; and iv) illustrate research results - 'team working'. These skills are acquired through presenting literature data and work, individual or group, produced during exercises and teaching laboratories, as well as during the internship. During the internship, the graduate must regularly present both literature data and results obtained from their laboratory and/or data processing activities within journal clubs organized by respective supervisors. Graduates also participate, where possible, in conferences, where abstract presentations and oral or poster communications are encouraged, allowing them to interact with scientists and professionals in their fields of interest.
Verification of achieving the objective of this descriptor will occur within in-course assessments, journal clubs, final course exams, and the final exam.
Official teaching and assessment languages.
ITALIAN, ENGLISH V - Learning abilities The graduate will acquire adequate learning abilities, particularly regarding consultation of specialized databases, innovative technologies, and critical reading and analysis of scientific publications. This will occur through frontal teaching activities and other training activities provided, both within individual courses and during laboratory and exercise activities.
Verification of achieving adequate learning ability will be conducted within in-course assessments, journal clubs, final course exams, and the final exam.
Competencies associated with the role.
Responsible for research lines and laboratories in analysis, biotechnology and food sectors in public and private entities Selection and use of methods for evaluating, certifying, managing, and conserving biological and environmental quality and biodiversity, particularly in the context of food microbiological and toxicological analysis, molecular diagnostics, quality control of biological origin products, and quality control and certification.
Ability to synthesize and disseminate scientific knowledge externally.
Independent professional biologist Environmental impact assessments, recovery plans, management plans, environmental restoration, biomonitoring for environmental quality assessment and study of natural population dynamics.
Assessment of conservation status of habitats and species included in international directives and national laws. Assessment of biological damage to cultural goods. Control and evaluation of biological quality and forensic expertise.
Design and management of food education programs for general subjects or specific groups of individuals, in physiological and pathological conditions, across different ages and with or without sports activity. Assessment and control of origin, nutritional quality, and toxicological aspects of food in chemical/biochemical contexts and in relation to national and community legislation on food policies, hygiene, and food control.
Passing the State Exam and registration with the Biologists' Register are necessary for practicing the independent profession of Biologist.
Role in work context.
Responsible for research lines and laboratories in analysis, biotechnology and food sectors in public and private entities Organization, direction, and coordination of biomolecular and biodiversity analyses. Chemical, biochemical, and molecular analyses in functional, qualitative, and toxicological evaluation; development and enhancement of functional foods and supplements supporting biomedical activities and sports, and maintaining optimal health status.
Organization and management in the food industry and other activities related to food distribution, transformation, and service.
Evaluation, planning, implementation, and control of a research project.
Scientific dissemination.

Final Project Characteristics The activities related to preparing the final project for the Master's degree in Biodiversity, Conservation and Environmental Quality are carried out by the student under the supervision of one or more tutor professors in the form of an internship at a university laboratory or a public or private external entity contracted with the University.
The objective of the internship is for the student to acquire in-depth knowledge of experimental methodology, analytical tools, and techniques for data analysis and processing.
The final project consists of presenting an original thesis developed by the student under the guidance of the supervisor. The final grade is expressed on a scale of 110 with possible honors.
Required Knowledge for Admission To access the Master's Degree Course in Biodiversity, Conservation and Environmental Quality, it is necessary to hold a degree or a three-year university diploma, or another title obtained abroad and recognized as suitable.
To be admitted to the Master's Degree Course, it is necessary to possess certain academic requirements and an adequate personal preparation.
Admission academic requirements are met by holding a degree in one of the following classes of D.M. 270/2004 (or corresponding in the former D.M. 509/99):
L-13 (Biological Sciences)
L-32 (Environmental and Natural Sciences)
L-2 (Biotechnology).
Admission is also permitted with a suitable title in a different degree class, provided that:
a) at least 66 ECTS in basic biological disciplines (BIO/01, BIO/02, BIO/04, BIO/05, BIO/06, BIO/07, BIO/09, BIO/10, BIO/11, BIO/18, BIO/19), 12 ECTS in basic chemical disciplines (CHIM/01, CHIM/02, CHIM/03, CHIM/06), and 15 ECTS in basic mathematical, physical, and computer science disciplines (MAT/01-09, FIS/01-08, and INF/01), in accordance with the guidelines of the Italian University Biologists College (CBUI);
b) a degree grade not lower than 100/110
For graduates from foreign universities, the suitability of academic requirements is assessed on a case-by-case basis based on the consistency between programs completed in different disciplinary areas, the foundational knowledge deemed necessary for the advanced training offered by the course, as well as language skills.
Additionally, possession of an English language certification at the B2 level of the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (CEFR) is required.
For foreign students, verification of adequate knowledge of the Italian language is required. Students who do not possess these language skills must attend specific courses to reach the required level within the additional training activities.
Personal preparation verification is mandatory and will be conducted through tests or interviews, following the procedures outlined in the course's academic regulations. Graduates who meet the academic requirements and have obtained their degree with a grade not lower than 95/110 will be exempt from this test.
Knowledge and Understanding. General Area Master's graduates who successfully complete the course will have acquired knowledge related to the study of biodiversity, from the molecular to the ecosystem level, and will have understood the mechanisms regulating processes, interactions, and the effects of various environmental parameters on living organisms.
Graduates will possess the knowledge and methodological foundations for studying biological and cultural diversity to conduct monitoring and ecosystem management activities.
Such knowledge and understanding will be acquired and verified through participation in lectures, field and/or laboratory exercises, and other curricular activities, through internships at qualified research laboratories, and with the final project involving the discussion of an original work.
Learning activities may also be carried out abroad through agreements with various universities within the Erasmus program and other international mobility programs.
Biodiversity and Environment Area Master's graduates who successfully complete the course will have acquired knowledge on:
- microbial biodiversity,
- fungal biodiversity and its economic and ecological importance,
- plant biodiversity,
- terrestrial animal biodiversity,
- role, importance, and conservation of biodiversity in ecological systems.
Graduates may also acquire knowledge on:
- plant-animal interactions,
- legal foundations for nature protection,
- plant biotechnology,
- biodiversity monitoring techniques.
The main teaching tool is the lecture, optionally supplemented by experimental demonstrations and laboratory and/or field activities. Knowledge assessment is conducted through oral and/or written exams.
Biomolecular Area Master's graduates who successfully complete the course will have acquired knowledge on:
- biological diversity at morphological, genomic, and molecular levels,
- genomics and the role of genetic variability in evolution, particularly in eukaryotic organisms,
- biodiversity as a source of pharmacologically active substances,
- knowledge of the effects of biodiversity derivatives on human health,
- specific skills in the field of food traceability and authenticity.
The main teaching tool is the lecture, optionally supplemented by experimental demonstrations and laboratory activities. Knowledge assessment is conducted through oral and/or written exams.
Contextual Knowledge and Final Project Knowledge and understanding of scientific instrumentation, organization, and management of research laboratories in the ecological-environmental field, also using biomolecular-cellular methodologies.
Knowledge and understanding of practical tools for data and information acquisition and processing using computer tools.
Master's graduates must be able to fluently use the English language, both in written and oral form, with particular reference to disciplinary terminology.
Knowledge assessment is conducted through oral and/or written exams.
The preparation and discussion of the thesis represent an additional tool for verifying the knowledge acquired during the course of study.

CURRICULUM: Judgment Autonomy
SECTION: Judgment Autonomy
URL: https://unisi.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/11094

Judgment Autonomy.
The graduate of the Master's Degree Course in Biodiversity, Conservation and Environmental Quality will be able to independently collect, evaluate, process and interpret experimental data and information necessary to address with conscious judgment autonomy:
- Project, structure and personnel responsibility;
- Identification of new perspectives and strategies for sustainable development;
- Evaluation, interpretation and reprocessing of literature data;
- Social and bioethical implications in planning environmental interventions.
The actual possession of judgment autonomy is verified both in the discussion of the Master's thesis and through examination assessments for each course. Additionally, during internship, training activities, or further training activities, the student can demonstrate their ability to analyze applied problems and formulate solutions in a learning environment different from that experienced during lectures.
The evaluation of judgment autonomy, in addition to the writing and discussion of the Master's thesis, occurs through written and oral tests, preparation of summaries, and thematic presentations.

Learning Ability.
The Master's Degree Course in Biodiversity, Conservation and Environmental Quality is designed to develop learning abilities that enable Master's graduates of the class to independently continue further studies in this field. Through formal teaching and other training activities provided both within individual courses and during the internship period, the Master's graduate in Biodiversity, Conservation and Environmental Quality will acquire adequate abilities for the continuous development and deepening of competencies, with particular reference to consulting specialized databases, learning innovative technologies, and updating specific knowledge through reading and critical analysis of scientific publications.

The verification of achieving the objective of this descriptor will occur within in-course assessments, 'journal club' sessions, examinations at the end of training activities, and the final assessment.

Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding.
Generic Area Master's graduates who have successfully completed the course of study must:
a. possess skills useful for analyzing genetic, taxonomic and ecosystem diversity;
b. possess skills in biomolecular and bioinformatics methodologies applied to the study of the variety of life forms and their interactions;
c. have fully mastered the scientific method, particularly for the purpose of evaluating environmental quality, biodiversity analysis, and conservation and management of species and habitats.
These competencies will be acquired and verified using scientific articles with both theoretical and experimental content as study material, as well as through practical laboratory and field activities, projects, and individual and group assignments focused on the analysis of concrete and current cases and problems. Particular emphasis will also be placed on verifying these competencies during the assessment of the final thesis.

Biodiversity and Environment Area The acquired knowledge enables the graduate to choose and use tools for applying analytical methodologies aimed at research in the field of biodiversity and environmental quality, and to develop abilities for analyzing, processing and communicating obtained data, also through the use of computer tools.
The final objective is the formation of a Master's graduate capable, independently within themes related to biodiversity and the environment, of:
- using techniques for investigating and monitoring animal and plant biodiversity in relation to various environmental contexts,
- formulating synthetic judgments on environmental quality based on biodiversity data,
- applying methodologies in the context of environmental assessment and disputes,
- planning the management and conservation of biodiversity,
- carrying out professional activities in the various application areas of biodiversity and environment, also assuming responsibility for projects and structures in both public and private sectors.

Biomolecular Area It is expected that the Master's graduate develops the professional abilities required for entering the workforce, particularly the necessary abilities to choose and use tools for applying analytical methodologies aimed at biomolecular and cellular research, and to develop the ability to analyze, process and present obtained data, also through the use of computer tools.
The acquisition of knowledge in biomolecular and cellular courses enables the Master's graduate to:
- prepare protocols for phenotypic and molecular study of unicellular organisms,
- formulate simple models for studying and understanding biological processes related to microbial biodiversity,
- conduct scientific research in biomolecular, bioinformatics and biostatistics fields applied to various areas of biodiversity and environmental biology,
- conduct risk/benefit assessments of xenobiotics,
- apply molecular methodologies for food quality and safety control.
The final objective is the formation of a Master's graduate capable of working with broad autonomy in the biomolecular-cellular field, also assuming responsibility for projects concerning biodiversity in both public and private sectors.

Contextual Knowledge and Final Assessment The acquisition of contextual knowledge enables the Master's graduate to possess the ability to:
- read and understand scientific documents, European regulations in English;
- plan experimental and observational studies, data collection, processing and analysis;
- write technical reports in English on obtained results;
- critically present and discuss their results;
- apply acquired knowledge in the workplace of laboratories, research institutions, and public and private companies in the ecological-environmental field.

Communication Skills.
The Master's graduate in Biodiversity, Conservation and Environmental Quality acquires adequate competencies and tools for communication, referring to the ability to present fluently in English using disciplinary terminology, ability to develop and present research and development projects, ability to organize group work, ability to illustrate research results ('team working'). These competencies are acquired both through the presentation of literature data as an integral part of each course, and during the internship. During this period, the graduate must regularly present both literature data and data obtained within 'journal club' organized by respective supervisors. Verification of achieving the objective of this descriptor will occur within in-course assessments, 'journal club', final exams after training activities, and the final thesis.

Description of specific training objectives.
The Master's Degree Course in Biodiversity, Conservation and Environmental Quality aims to provide advanced preparation in environmental biology regarding biodiversity, from the molecular to the ecosystem level, through a training path that provides methodological and cultural foundations for biodiversity conservation and environmental quality assessment. Having in-depth knowledge of the scientific investigation method, with particular regard to techniques for acquiring and analyzing biodiversity data, and being able to work with broad autonomy are indispensable requirements for the Master's graduate in Biodiversity, Conservation and Environmental Quality.
To promote the dissemination of knowledge and offer students more easily marketable training paths, courses are delivered in English and English language proficiency at B2 level is required upon entry.
The Master's Degree Course in Biodiversity, Conservation and Environmental Quality is structured through three main thematic areas: 1) Biodiversity and Environment Area; 2) Biomolecular Area; 3) Contextual Knowledge and Final Thesis.
1) Biodiversity and Environment Area includes courses and activities for acquiring: i) scientific knowledge in environmental biology, with particular reference to the analysis of animal, plant, and microbial biodiversity; ii) in-depth knowledge of biodiversity monitoring and management and environmental quality, including legislative aspects; iii) ability to monitor and analyze biotic components of natural and artificial ecosystems; iv) specific competencies for the analysis, assessment, and conservation of biological components of the territory.
2) Biomolecular Area includes courses and activities relevant for acquiring: i) in-depth knowledge of biological diversity at morphological, genomic, and molecular levels; ii) knowledge of methodological and cultural foundations of scientific research in biomolecular, bioinformatics, and biostatistics fields applied to various biodiversity and environmental biology contexts; iii) knowledge of the effects of biodiversity derivatives on human health; iv) specific competencies in the field of food traceability and authenticity.
3) Contextual Knowledge and Final Thesis represent the completion of the training path for obtaining the Master's Degree in Biodiversity, Conservation and Environmental Quality. Contextual knowledge is achieved through: i) participation in field and laboratory experimental activities; ii) planning of experimental and observational studies, data collection, processing, and analysis; iii) a final thesis based on work carried out during the internship period related to various aspects of biodiversity monitoring and conservation and environmental quality, presented in an original thesis organized according to internationally accepted scientific community standards.

Admission Requirements Candidates possessing a degree issued by an Italian university in one of the following classes: L-7 Civil and Environmental Engineering L-8 Information Engineering L-9 Industrial Engineering L-30 Physics and Technology Sciences L-31 Computer and Information Technology Sciences L-35 Mathematical Sciences L-41 Statistics with a grade above a threshold specified in the course's academic regulations, are directly admitted to the Master's Degree course in Computer and Automation Engineering.
Professional status conferred by the title. Intelligent Systems Engineer The Master's graduate in Artificial Intelligence and Automation Engineering naturally finds placement within companies, public bodies, and research centers, at national or international levels, engaged in the design, development, and management of complex intelligent systems. The Study Course also allows for autonomous professional activities as a consultant.
Automation Engineer The Master's graduate in Artificial Intelligence and Automation Engineering naturally finds placement within companies, public bodies, and research centers, at national or international levels, engaged in the design, development, and management of industrial and robotic automation systems, or complex systems integrating the typical components of information engineering. The Study Course also allows for autonomous professional activities as a consultant.
Final Exam Characteristics The final exam requires the preparation and discussion of a thesis (Master's Thesis), prepared by the student in an original manner under the guidance of a supervisor, possibly assisted by one or more co-supervisors.
The Master's Thesis can be compilative or theoretical-experimental. In any case, the final exam aims to highlight the student's acquired abilities for studying, understanding, critically evaluating, and designing advanced and original solutions in the scientific/technological field. Synthesis skills, scientific rigor, and organization in preparing the thesis and presenting the work orally, scheduled at the end of the study path, will also be evaluated.
In the case of a theoretical-experimental thesis, the Academic Committee appoints a counter-supervisor, whose task is to evaluate the candidate's original contribution and the organization of the thesis.
The Master's Thesis can be written in English, Italian, or an official language of the EU.
It is possible to carry out part of the activities related to the final exam within an internship or traineeship at companies, organizations, or research laboratories.
Required Knowledge for Access Access to the study course is reserved for holders of a three-year university degree or diploma, or another title acquired abroad and recognized as suitable. Access requires candidates to meet curricular and personal preparation requirements. It is not possible to enroll with academic deficiencies at entry.
Curricular Requirements A degree in one of the following classes is required: - L-7 Civil and Environmental Engineering (8) - L-8 Information Engineering (9) - L-9 Industrial Engineering (10) - L-30 Physics and Technology Sciences (25) - L-31 Computer and Information Technology Sciences (26) - L-35 Mathematical Sciences (32) or an equivalent class according to the former D.M. 509/99 (the equivalent class number is indicated in parentheses).
Curricular requirements are also satisfied by holders of a specialist degree under D.M. 509/99 or a degree under the previous D.M. 509/99 framework, in engineering, mathematical, and physical disciplines, subject to the Academic Committee's evaluation of an appropriate differentiation of the educational objectives of such study paths compared to the Master's program.
For students holding a degree issued by a foreign university, the evaluation of curricular requirements is entrusted to the Academic Committee, which particularly verifies: - that the degree is issued upon completion of a study course of at least three years; - that the educational objectives are sufficiently comparable to those of one of the above-mentioned degree classes.
English language knowledge at least B2 level of the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages is required.
Non-Italian native students who do not reach at least level A1 of Italian language knowledge must include in their study plans training activities aimed at achieving this level.
Personal Preparation Requirements Admission to the Study Course, for students possessing the curricular requirements, is subject to verification of personal preparation, according to the methods defined in the Course's Academic Regulations. The verification concerns knowledge in the disciplinary fields of mathematics, statistics, physics, and information engineering. For students holding a specialist degree under D.M. 509/99 or a degree under the previous D.M. 509/99 framework, the verification of personal preparation requirements will be evaluated on a case-by-case basis by the Academic Committee.
For students holding a degree obtained abroad, the Academic Committee conducts a selection that includes evaluation of personal preparation based on the study curriculum and a written and/or oral admission test.

Judgment Autonomy.
The Master's graduate in Artificial Intelligence and Automation Engineering must be able to make quantitative assessments based on the acquired methodological and technical knowledge. They must also be able to evaluate the possible effects, costs, and validity of different solutions compared to those used to solve known problems, leveraging new opportunities promoted by technological development. This capability will be enabled by mastery of characteristic technical/scientific tools of the fields of competence and the habit of analyzing complex systems characterized by conflicting requirements and imperfect adherence to reference theoretical models. Fundamental means to develop independence and critical awareness will be the development of projects assigned for more applied courses, both characteristic and related, and the elaboration of the final thesis, in which the student must demonstrate having acquired autonomy in choice and project capacity in innovative technological fields, using advanced tools. The acquisition of adequate judgment capacity is verified in the evaluation of developed projects and the discussion of the thesis.
Learning Capacity.
The Master's graduate in Artificial Intelligence and Automation Engineering must develop their own learning capacity in order to continue studying and updating, to be able to operate effectively in diverse work contexts, even in the presence of new and previously unaddressed situations. For this reason, the Master's graduate will have a broad view of the methodological, technical, and scientific landscape to refer to for studying and addressing complex and innovative problems. In particular, many characteristic and related courses, especially the thesis work, will require personal in-depth study to provide the ability to search for and select relevant literature and to study and learn state-of-the-art solutions. In the delivery of characteristic and related training activities, the overall workload for the student involves a prevalence of individual work hours over frontal teaching, to facilitate the development of student autonomy in personal subject deepening. Other useful tools for achieving this ability are internships carried out both in Italy and abroad. The achievement of adequate learning capacity is verified in examination tests requiring personal in-depth study, in activities carried out during the internship, and in results achieved in thesis preparation.

Communication Skills.
The master's graduate in Artificial Intelligence and Automation Engineering must be able to use their technical and foundational preparation to dialogue and communicate their ideas to a wide range of professional figures, with an appropriate and rigorous presentation style. They must also be able to interface with the research world to precisely present problems requiring innovative solutions and transfer such solutions to the production world. This type of skill is essential for the development and coordination of complex projects. These abilities will be acquired both through the drafting of technical documents for specific projects, as well as through presentations, and through an adequate introduction to the technical language used in the scientific literature of the sector, within the context of the examinations of the individual characteristic and/or related courses. The delivery of the course entirely in English will allow the student to directly acquire greater familiarity with the reference technical dictionary. Furthermore, the final exam offers the student an opportunity to deepen and verify their abilities in analysis, processing, and communication of the work carried out. It involves, in fact, the discussion, before a committee, of a work produced by the student on a thematic area covered during their study path. In this case, evaluation is not only on the content of the work, but also on the candidate's synthesis, communication, and presentation abilities, as well as the justification, even dialectical, of the choices made. The verification of achieving an adequate level of communication skills is therefore carried out in oral exams, in the evaluation of technical reports of projects carried out, and in the writing and presentation of the thesis.

They can carry out activities in various application contexts, dealing with aspects ranging from problem analysis and modeling, to the selection and evaluation of techniques to be used, to the design of algorithms and their software implementation, to the management, programming, and optimization of high-performance computing architectures, up to the search for innovative solutions and the creation of high-tech companies.

Additional information.
http://www.unisi.it Specific training objectives description.
The training path of the Master's Degree in Artificial Intelligence and Automation Engineering aims at deepening scientific methodologies and techniques necessary for formulating and studying complex engineering problems, and seeks to provide advanced knowledge on the main technologies and applications in the fields of computer systems, artificial intelligence, industrial automation, and robotics. The course provides the necessary competencies for the design, management, development, and technological innovation in the field of intelligent systems and in the sector of control systems and robotics. In particular, the training paths focus on the issues of human-machine interaction in a broad sense, focusing on themes such as artificial intelligence, machine learning, high-performance processing for large data quantities, human-robot interfaces, and production automation systems. Furthermore, the course aims to provide the master's graduate with the tools and knowledge necessary to continue studies in a research doctorate in the area of information engineering.
The structure of the training offer allows focusing preparation on the design of intelligent systems or within the field of robotics and automation. The training paths are structured into the following learning areas.
Intelligent Systems Specific competencies in the field of computer engineering are provided through targeted training paths to deepen the techniques of artificial intelligence and machine learning necessary for designing and implementing intelligent systems. In particular, it is possible to deepen topics regarding the main methodological tools necessary to design, evaluate, and program parallel and high-performance computing architectures; methodologies for the design and implementation of complex software systems and distributed applications; design of systems for managing and analyzing large data volumes; language theory and technologies for natural language processing; bioinformatics and information systems for biological databases; image processing algorithms; optimization methodologies on networks.
Robotics and Automation Knowledge and competencies related to the design of robotic and industrial automation systems are provided. In particular, it is possible to deepen topics regarding human-robot interaction and haptic interfaces; methodologies and techniques for the analysis and design of discrete-event systems and multivariable and nonlinear control systems, with applications ranging from robot control to trajectory planning, up to multi-agent systems; techniques for modeling, analysis, and simulation of complex dynamic systems; elements of estimation theory applied to system identification and filtering of dynamic systems; paradigms of uncertainty representation and techniques for analysis and design of uncertain systems; network optimization methodologies; design of advanced sensors.
Contextual knowledge and final exam The student's preparation is completed by technical-practical competencies that can be acquired through internships or traineeships at organizations, sector companies, or research laboratories. Furthermore, the training activities allow the student to acquire good mastery of the technical language in English, enabling them to write reports and organize presentations of their work. The final exam allows the student to put into practice the acquired knowledge by autonomously addressing the design of an advanced technological solution.

Professional status conferred by the degree.
Archaeologist
The Master's Degree in Archaeology allows for career opportunities in:
- Public institutions and bodies responsible for excavation, conservation, and valorization of archaeological heritage, such as Superintendencies, Museums, and Archaeological Parks;
- Public and private institutions and bodies engaged in the study, research, and cultural dissemination of archaeological heritage, such as local authorities and Foundations;
- Companies, work cooperatives, or specialized enterprises in consultancy and services for Archaeological Heritage.
It is specified that for certain high-responsibility positions (e.g., at Superintendencies, directorial roles in MIBACT, direction of Archaeological Museums, research institutions, etc.), additional post-graduate qualifications (Research Doctorates, Specialization Schools, Master's Degrees) are required.
Final Exam Characteristics The final exam consists of a public discussion before a committee composed of a number of professors specified in the University and Department Regulations, of a thesis produced from original research and the result of a personal synthesis of knowledge acquired during the training path.
The thesis and its discussion must demonstrate the candidate's ability to independently use specific sources of their field of study, relevant research tools, and the necessary knowledge resources to produce an original work that represents a significant advancement in the field. They must also demonstrate the candidate's ability to clearly and effectively present and adequately argue the results of their research.
The thesis work will be carried out under the supervision of one of the course professors and will be discussed with the participation of a counter-reviewer.
The final exam evaluation will be expressed on a scale of 110 with possible honors. In addition to considering the average of the grades obtained during the studies, the merit score is mainly attributed based on the methodological rigor and originality of the research work.
Required Knowledge for Access Candidates possessing a Master's Degree or a three-year University Diploma or another foreign degree deemed suitable are admitted to the Master's Degree Course in Archaeology.
Additionally, students must possess specific curricular requirements, adequate personal preparation including knowledge of the English language at B1 level.
Curricular requirements are satisfied by holding a degree in one of the following degree classes (ex DM 270/2004 or ex DM 509/1999 or another equivalent foreign degree):
Cultural Heritage (L-1);
Letters (L-10);
Technologies for the Conservation and Restoration of Cultural Heritage (L-43);
Letters (5);
Sciences of Cultural Heritage (13);
Technologies for the Conservation and Restoration of Cultural Heritage (41).
Graduates in the listed classes must also have earned at least 54 CFU in the following scientific-disciplinary sectors: BIO/08, ICAR/19, INF/01, L-ANT/01, L-ANT/02, L-ANT/03, L-ANT/04, L-ANT/05, L-ANT/06, L-ANT/07, L-ANT/08, L-ANT/09, L-ANT/10, L-ART/04, L-FIL-LET/01, L-OR/05, M-DEA/01, M-GGR/01, M-STO/01; basic computer skills at least equivalent to ECDL core are also required.
Curricular requirements are also satisfied for graduates in degree classes different from those previously listed, provided they have earned at least 60 CFU in the following scientific-disciplinary sectors: BIO/08, ICAR/19, INF/01, L-ANT/01, L-ANT/02 L-ANT/03, L-ANT/04, L-ANT/05, L-ANT/06, L-ANT/07, L-ANT/08, L-ANT/09, L-ANT/10, L-ART/04, L-FIL-LET/01, L-OR/05, M-DEA/01, M-GGR/01, M-STO/01; basic computer skills at least equivalent to ECDL core are also required.
Personal preparation is then verified through an interview, accessible only to students possessing the curricular requirements. The methods of verifying personal preparation are defined in the Teaching Regulations of the Master's Degree Course.
Degree Awarded.
Master's Degree in Archaeology
Teaching Delivery Mode Conventional
Knowledge and Understanding.
Generic Area The training path for students in the Master's Degree course aims at building and developing a solid professional preparation through the delivery of courses dedicated to deepening the procedures and purposes of research, protection, conservation, and valorization of archaeology. The training space allowed by the two-year program will enable the student to identify a Study Plan whose content is proposed within discipline aggregations created with logical sense, identifiable in chronological order within the three macrothemes of Prehistoric Archaeology, Classical Archaeology, and Medieval Archaeology. The student will also be guided in constructing their own Study Plan to reach a higher level of depth in their area of interest, subject to approval by the Teaching Committee of the Master's Degree Course in Archaeology.
Based on these design lines, the Course offers a two-year program:
Year 1 The student will be able to acquire a solid cultural foundation on the archaeologies of the Mediterranean and European areas in relation to the themes of Prehistoric and Protohistoric Archaeology, Classical Archaeology, and Medieval Archaeology. Some in-depth topics will cover: historical, philological, and demo-ethno-anthropological disciplines; musealization and management of archaeological heritage; the most advanced methodologies applied to landscape archaeology, excavation techniques, reading and interpretation of archaeological contexts, and the most modern archaeological technologies.
Year 2 Specific in-depth topics are provided, offering the student further historical, archaeological, computer, and legislative competencies in the archaeological sector. In the second year, the student has the opportunity to deepen field experience through participation in excavations, experimental research projects, internships, and training internships, along with acquiring language skills and preparing a final exam, preparatory for obtaining the Master's Degree title.
Methodology and Understanding of Archaeological Sources Traditional investigation and study tools and new methodologies and technologies
Archaeological and Monumental Heritage Process data and construct interpretive models
Autonomy of Judgment.
Graduates of the Master's Degree course will acquire a confident ability for autonomous judgment, which will manifest particularly in:
* using the knowledge, skills, abilities, and capacities acquired during the studies to express autonomous, articulated, motivated, and original judgments on specific issues within the disciplines and area of interest;
* the ability to manage in a conscious and critical manner the diversity of possible interdisciplinary and multidisciplinary approaches to build new research topics and new methods of conducting research;
* the ability to confidently navigate within the theoretical and methodological reflection related to the area of interest;
* the ability to critically treat different source systems to preliminarily evaluate their overall reliability and usability for research purposes, also in reference to the qualitative and quantitative aspects of the statistical sample they represent;
* the ability to evaluate and explicitly state the social value of scientific research on the past of humanity understood in the broadest and most articulated sense.
Teaching Methods and Tools for Achieving Objectives:
Specific courses or specific segments within the curricular courses dedicated to the theoretical-methodological aspects of different disciplines and issues of interoperability between similar disciplinary fields.
Assessment Methods:
Evaluation of judgment maturity regarding these aspects within the curricular exams, also through the discussion of independent works.
Learning Ability.
Graduates of the Master's Degree course will have fully developed all learning abilities (linguistic, lexical, dialectical, argumentative, etc.) that enable them to continue their training process at more advanced levels. In particular:
* the ability to use bibliographic tools in traditional form and/or with the support of new technologies in absolute autonomy;
* the ability to participate in a conscious, critical, and active manner in advanced training sessions within formal courses or during events of different nature (seminars, conferences, etc.);
* the ability to outline their own path in the development of the training process, selecting the most suitable training opportunities to achieve the set cognitive, research, and professional goals.
Teaching Methods and Tools for Achieving Objectives:
Specific segments within the disciplinary courses dedicated to illustrating the main tools and procedures for individual research, also with the aid of computer resources;
Seminar activities at various levels
Assessment Methods:
Verification of achieved skills in this area through the evaluation of written and audiovisual works and the degree of active participation in the planned teaching and seminar activities.
Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding.
Generic Area Graduates of the Master's Degree course will be able to apply the complex of acquired knowledge and understanding capabilities in:
* Construction of an individual cultural identity and a solid professional approach to work in various activity areas (research, protection, valorization, training, dissemination, etc.);
* Identification of research areas and potentially fruitful issues in the field of archaeological disciplines related to antiquity in its broadest sense, to be investigated through the development of independent research projects;
* Creation and management of small work groups aimed at conducting independent research in the areas of interest;
* Creation and management of innovative research tools related to the application of new technologies to archaeological disciplines;
* Design and implementation of diverse forms of public communication (scientific and popular publications, new media, events, etc.) in relation to the area of interest.
Teaching Methods and Tools for Achieving Objectives:
Segments of the curricular courses specifically aimed at developing methodological reflection.
Seminar activities and applied research on-site and in the laboratory.
Assessment Methods:
Curricular exams.
Evaluation of participation in seminar activities and field and laboratory research.
Methodology and Understanding of Archaeological Sources Application of the most appropriate procedures for studying and interpreting archaeological data, using the most advanced methodologies and techniques, accessible to students during field research and laboratory exercises.
Archaeological and Monumental Heritage The final goal is to achieve the necessary skills to understand the historical, material, and artistic aspects of archaeological and monumental heritage and to propose its appropriate valorization.

Communication skills.
Master's degree graduates will have acquired advanced and articulated communication skills enabling them to:
* clearly and thoroughly communicate their ideas – in written, oral, and/or new media formats – to diverse audiences (specialists in the relevant disciplinary field, interested public, general public), clearly highlighting in their discourse the relationship between the data base used and the interpretative inferences derived from it;
* develop innovative communication tools that fully exploit the potential offered by new technologies in the fields of public communication, education, and the creation of data bases and operational tools aimed at advancing research in their specific field of interest;
* integrate – through the conscious and critical use of a shared specialized language – into an international scientific community.
Teaching methods and tools to achieve the objectives:
Use of the most advanced technologies in the comprehensive management of archaeological data.
Use of critical text anthologies in Italian and the main languages of the international scientific community for didactic purposes, in relation to different disciplinary fields.
Assessment methods:
Evaluation, during exams, during active participation in teaching and seminar activities, and during the production of written works, of the ability to understand/speak in a rich specialized language and to fully understand critical texts even in languages other than Italian.
Planned employment and professional opportunities for graduates.
Archaeologist The Master's Degree in Archaeology enables employment opportunities in:
- Public institutions and bodies responsible for excavation, conservation, and valorization of archaeological heritage, such as Superintendencies, Museums, and Archaeological Parks;
- Public and private institutions and bodies engaged in the study, research, and dissemination of archaeological heritage, such as local authorities and Foundations;
- Companies, cooperatives, or specialized firms providing consultancy and services for Archaeological Heritage.
It is specified that for certain roles requiring higher responsibility (e.g., at Superintendencies, directorial functions in MIBACT, direction of Archaeological Museums, research bodies, etc.), additional post-graduate qualifications (PhD programs, Specialization Schools, Masters) are required.
Official teaching and assessment languages.
ITALIANO Associated competencies for the role.
Archaeologist
- Competencies in coordinating and organizing study and research projects, national and international, based on archaeological foundations with historical-cultural objectives;
- Competencies in managing the technical, legislative, and interpretative aspects of an archaeological site, without neglecting organizational aspects related to worker safety;
- Competencies in organizing and managing research activities at a territorial level, within the framework of a detailed reconstruction of the archaeological landscape;
- Competencies in understanding and evaluating the conservation status of an archaeological context, identifying potential restoration interventions;
- Information technology and technological competencies;
- Competencies in designing forms of valorization, accessibility, and dissemination of archaeological heritage.
Description of admission tests.
1. For admission to the Master's Degree in Archaeology, the verification of the student's personal preparation will be conducted through selective tests organized by the competent teaching structures.
2. Specifically, the admission test consists of an interview with three professors designated annually by the Teaching Committee, focusing on the candidate's knowledge of Italian, European, and Mediterranean archaeology from prehistory to the post-medieval period. The test is considered passed if the candidate demonstrates good chronological orientation and sufficient critical reading ability of the archaeological contexts discussed.
3. The admission test may be held in one or more sessions. If multiple sessions are scheduled, those not admitted in the first session may reapply for the next session.
4. The test is open to graduates meeting the curricular requirements and to students in their final year who have acquired at least 120 CFU by the test date.
5. Students who have passed the verification test will be admitted conditionally and may enroll provided they obtain their degree within the deadlines for enrollment closure.
Direct admission
1. Graduates who, meeting the curricular requirements, have obtained a final grade of not less than 100/110 are exempt from the admission test.
2. Additionally, Master's degree graduates meeting the curricular requirements are exempt from the admission test.
Role in the workplace context.
Archaeologist Considering that the profession of archaeologist is not currently recognized by any national regulation and lacks a specific professional register, the archaeologist studies, from a historical perspective, material culture, ritual and funerary aspects of communities from Prehistory to the Middle Ages; forms of product distribution and trade; circulation of people and relationships between cultures; interaction of human groups with the environment and its resources, and the formation and evolution of the ancient landscape. The archaeologist also has the opportunity to intervene in the actions of protection, valorization, and accessibility of archaeological heritage, also from the perspective of dissemination and education. Furthermore, the social role of the archaeologist as a cultural mediator to transmit historical knowledge, characteristics, and traditions of territories to increasingly heterogeneous communities by geographical origin is noteworthy. Finally, the archaeologist can work towards understanding, at increasingly complex levels, the historical, cultural, and anthropological nature of an administrative territory (municipal, provincial, or regional), promoting the recognition of local peculiarities and their relationship with external realities. The Master's Degree in Archaeology serves as a prerequisite for accessing high-level specialization paths (PhD programs, Specialization Schools, Masters) necessary to obtain the qualifications required by institutions such as Superintendencies, Archaeological Museums, Research Bodies, or to continue research in an academic context.
Additional information.
http://www.unisi.it/dipartimenti/dipartimento-scienze-storiche-e-dei-beni-culturali Specific educational objectives description.
The Master's Degree in Archaeology aims to prepare and guide students to recognize the complexity of archaeological work, balancing classroom and laboratory training with the stimulation to work in groups on increasingly complex research topics, grounded in the ability to identify sites, archaeological contexts, material productions, and landscapes as part of a more articulated cultural and historical context. The field of archaeological disciplines is undergoing significant transformation in response to the need to sensitize and connect with contemporary society and the world. The Study Program emphasizes the high and potential social value of archaeological work as an essential mediator in the complexity of contemporary society, to deepen the historical identity of communities, which are increasingly transient and fragmented, providing them with tools to deeply appreciate the stratification of urban, rural, and cultural landscapes. Particular attention is given in the training path to fieldwork, with participation in research projects directed by professors, to which students are invited to actively contribute from the end of the first year. Training internships and practical training in the second year help and guide integration into the workplace. Master's Degree in Archaeology students are offered the opportunity to acquire disciplinary, methodological, and operational competencies in the field of Italian, European, and Mediterranean archaeology (from Prehistory to the Middle Ages), with knowledge of traditional investigation tools and new sector technologies (through core courses in SSD L-ANT/01, L-ANT/06, L-ANT/07, L-ANT/08, L-ANT/09, L-ANT/10). The goal is to enable students to acquire skills and competencies in using different sources of archaeological, historical, epigraphic, and technical nature for reconstructing the ancient world, with specific references to areas of applied legislation for archaeological heritage, conservation, musealization, and management of cultural heritage, leveraging competencies in the use of information technologies and telecommunication tools in various potential application fields for archaeological heritage (through courses in SSD L-ANT/02, L-ANT/03, M-STO/01, IUS/10, GEO/07, BIO/08, CHIM/12, M-DEA/01). Fluency in written and oral English is also required. The program is structured over two years: the first year aims to provide a solid cultural foundation regarding the archaeologies of the Mediterranean and European areas on topics of Prehistoric and Protohistoric Archaeology, Classical Archaeology, and Medieval Archaeology, allowing the acquisition or deepening of knowledge in historical, iconographic, technological, archaeometric, and anthropological disciplines. The second year allows students to choose the direction in which to deepen their knowledge, identifying a path that prioritizes the acquisition of additional archaeological competencies in the Prehistoric and Protohistoric, Classical, or Medieval fields, with references also to areas of protection, conservation, and valorization of archaeological heritage, its musealization, and accessibility. Final exam characteristics The final exam requires the writing and defense of a thesis (Master's Thesis), developed by the student in an original manner under the guidance of a supervisor, possibly assisted by one or more co-supervisors.
The Master's Thesis can be compilative or theoretical-experimental. In any case, the final exam aims to highlight the student's acquired abilities for studying, understanding, critically evaluating and designing advanced and original solutions in the scientific/technological field. Synthesis abilities, methodological rigor and organization in drafting the work and presenting it orally at the end of the study program will also be assessed.
The Teaching Committee appoints a counter-supervisor, whose task is to evaluate the original contribution of the candidate and the organization of the work. The Master's Thesis can be written in English, Italian or an official language of the European Union. It is possible to carry out part of the activities related to the final exam within an internship or traineeship at companies, organizations or research laboratories.
Required knowledge for admission Admission to the study program is reserved for holders of a three-year university degree or equivalent foreign qualification recognized as suitable. Admission requires candidates to meet curricular and personal preparation requirements. It is not possible to enroll with academic debt at entry.

Degree in class L35 (Mathematical Sciences) or class L-32 under D.M. 509/99.

together with having earned a minimum number of CFU in the MAT/xx fields, as defined in the Course Regulations.
For students whose degree was issued by a foreign university, the curricular requirements assessment is handled by the Teaching Committee, which verifies: that the qualification was issued after a study program of at least three years; that the studies followed are adequate compared to the requirements of the above-mentioned degree classes.
English language knowledge at least B2 level of the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages is required.
Non-Italian native speakers who do not reach at least A1 level of Italian language knowledge must include in their study plans training activities aimed at achieving this level.
Personal preparation requirements Admission to the Study Program, for students meeting curricular requirements, is conditional on verifying personal preparation, according to the procedures defined in the Course Regulations.
For students with foreign qualifications, the Teaching Committee conducts a selection involving evaluation of personal preparation based on the study curriculum and a written and/or oral entrance exam.
Knowledge and understanding.
Mathematical Methods Master's graduates in Applied Mathematics acquire additional knowledge that complements their basic mathematical skills, covering all major areas of mathematics (mathematical logic, algebra, geometry, mathematical analysis, mathematical physics, statistics, numerical analysis, optimization) fundamental for addressing complex and stimulating challenges in mathematics and beyond. Subsequently, students can choose courses focused on:
- in-depth study of specific areas of pure mathematics, introducing new recent developments and research problems in mathematics, particularly in Logic, Algebra, Geometry, Mathematical Analysis;
- topics where advanced mathematical methods are essential in recent scientific research and technological development.
In particular, students gain knowledge of modern mathematical theories and the problems they address, along with continuous updating capabilities through reading advanced texts and scientific journals.
Mathematical Models The Study Program includes some courses that complete basic mathematical skills, covering areas of Mathematics necessary for deepening applied topics (Mathematical Analysis, Geometry, Statistics, Numerical Analysis, Optimization). Subsequently, students can choose courses with more applied content, including the study of data analysis, artificial intelligence and machine learning applications, bioinformatics and information systems to understand modeling, analysis and simulation techniques of processes derived from other scientific disciplines, such as engineering, physics, biology or medicine.
Students are thus trained to interact with professors and researchers working in scientific and technological fields requiring advanced mathematical tools. The acquired skills include the ability to retrieve methodological information from advanced mathematical literature.
Achievement of objectives is assessed in the final exams of the courses and through the final exam.

Critical Judgment.
Master's graduates in Applied Mathematics are able to:
know how to connect different mathematical concepts, keeping in mind the logical and hierarchical structure of mathematics;
critically analyze a proof, and produce a standard one when necessary;
evaluate the appropriateness of a mathematical model or theory in describing a concrete phenomenon;
conduct independent bibliographic research using mathematical content books, also developing familiarity with sector scientific journals;
use available electronic archives for scientific research on the WEB, performing the necessary information selection;
understand and evaluate the difficulties of the teaching/learning process based on the topic treated and the students' situation;
possess an adequate level of awareness of the possible ethical and social implications of their own activity.
These objectives will be achieved through activities provided for all courses (lectures, individual study, written and oral exams). Additionally, using specific mathematical and applied courses, students will be exposed to the latest developments in research in both pure and applied mathematics. The verification of acquiring adequate judgment capacity is assessed in the evaluation of problem-solving ability in exams and in the discussion of the thesis.
Learning Ability.
Master's graduates in Applied Mathematics must develop their own learning ability in order to continue studying and updating themselves, to effectively operate in various work contexts, even in the presence of new and previously unaddressed situations. Therefore, Master's graduates will have a broad view of the methodological and scientific landscape to refer to when studying and addressing complex and innovative mathematical problems. In particular, many courses, both characteristic and related, especially the thesis work, will require personal in-depth study to provide the ability to search for and select relevant literature and to study and learn state-of-the-art solutions. In the delivery of characteristic and related training activities, the overall workload for the student involves a prevalence of individual work hours over frontal teaching, to facilitate the development of student autonomy in personal subject deepening. The verification of achieving adequate learning ability is carried out in exam exercises requiring personal in-depth study, in activities carried out during the internship, and in the results achieved in thesis preparation.
Master's graduates in Applied Mathematics are therefore able to continue their studies, both in Mathematics and in other related disciplines, with a high degree of autonomy. They have a flexible mindset, solid preparation, and are able to quickly integrate into work environments, easily adapting to new issues.
Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding.
Mathematical Methods Students acquire a solid understanding of fundamental mathematical theories, including mathematical analysis, algebra, geometry, logic, numerical calculus, and probability theory. This in-depth knowledge is essential for developing new theories, models, and methodologies, as well as for applying mathematics to a wide range of sectors.
One of the main goals is to enable students to analyze and solve complex problems using advanced mathematical methods. Students learn to use sophisticated tools and techniques to address theoretical and applied problems, developing a rigorous and logical approach to problem-solving.
In addition to the ability to solve problems and understand complex theories, Mathematics graduates also develop critical and analytical thinking skills. These competencies allow them to critically evaluate proposed solutions, recognize patterns, and identify relationships between seemingly distinct mathematical concepts. This goal will also be achieved through the study of advanced texts and research articles in mathematics, both within courses and during the preparation of the final dissertation. The achievement of this goal is assessed in final course exams and in the final exam.
Another important aspect is the ability to communicate complex mathematical concepts clearly and concisely. Students learn to present their results in written and oral form, adapting language and level of detail to the target audience. This communication skill is crucial for collaborating with other mathematicians and conveying discoveries to a wide range of recipients.
Finally, Mathematics graduates develop an open and adaptable mindset that prepares them to face evolving challenges in academic, industrial, and technological worlds. They are able to quickly adapt to new contexts, new technologies, and new ideas, always maintaining an analytical and creative approach.
These objectives will be achieved through lectures, individual study, and written and oral exams provided for mandatory courses.
Mathematical Models The study path enables students to acquire a wide range of skills and abilities that are fundamental for addressing the complex challenges of the modern world. Through an interdisciplinary approach that combines theory and practice, students gain a solid foundation of mathematical knowledge and the ability to apply it in real contexts.
One of the main aspects of the acquired abilities is the ability to solve complex problems. Students learn to analyze, interpret, and solve mathematical problems using a wide range of tools and techniques. This skill is fundamental for addressing challenges in various sectors, from scientific research to engineering, from financial analysis to computational biology.
Additionally, students develop a deep understanding of mathematical theory and its applications. This includes solid knowledge of differential equations, probability theory and statistics, as well as advanced techniques in optimization and mathematical modeling. This in-depth understanding enables graduates to generate accurate and relevant models to address real-world problems.
Beyond technical competence, the Applied Mathematics degree also develops students' communication and teamwork abilities. Students learn to communicate their mathematical results clearly and concisely, both verbally and in writing, and to collaborate effectively with colleagues from different disciplines.
Finally, the Master's degree in Applied Mathematics prepares students to be flexible and adaptable in the face of new challenges and new technologies. The acquired skills are highly transferable and can be applied in a wide range of sectors, making graduates highly sought after in both academic and industrial worlds.
In conclusion, graduates of the Master's degree in Applied Mathematics at the University of Siena emerge with a solid foundation of knowledge and abilities that prepare them for a successful career in various fields, from scientific research to technological innovation, from financial analysis to business consulting.
These objectives will be achieved and verified through lectures, laboratory activities, written and oral exams, provided for optional course groups (which include a sufficient number of courses related to other scientific and technological areas), and through individual study, including that related to the preparation of the final dissertation, which may include an internship activity.

Communication Skills.
Master's graduates in Applied Mathematics:

The objective is gradually achieved through written and oral exams, as well as through the preparation of the final exam. Related and integrative training activities, which also belong to scientific/disciplinary fields not strictly mathematical, will help achieve this goal. The course being entirely taught in English will allow the student to directly acquire greater familiarity with the reference scientific terminology. Additionally, the final exam offers the student an opportunity to deepen and verify their analytical, processing, and communication skills. It involves the discussion, before a committee, of a work produced by the student on a thematic area covered during their study path. In this case, evaluation is not only on the content of the work but also on the candidate's synthesis, communication, and presentation skills, as well as the justification, even dialectical, of the choices made. The verification of achieving an adequate level of communication skills is therefore carried out in oral exams, in the evaluation of technical reports from projects completed, and in the writing and presentation of the thesis.

To this end, in the study path, the Master's graduate in Applied Mathematics, after completing theoretical preparation across all scientific-disciplinary fields of Mathematics, acquires advanced competencies in methods of discrete mathematics, applied algebra, differential systems, and mathematical modeling formalization, which are fundamental in applications especially (but not exclusively) in cross-disciplinary areas of modern science and technology, such as data processing (using mathematical techniques for studying artificial intelligence, information theory, and biological and financial databases) and modeling of complex systems (using mathematical techniques for studying nonlinear, discrete and continuous events systems and their representation).

They may hold coordination roles in research and development projects involving experts from other fields in an international context. They may complete their preparation for teaching in schools, pure and applied research in research institutions. Additionally, they may also play a role in disseminating scientific culture.
Additional information.
http://www.unisi.it Specific training objectives description.
The Master's degree training path in Applied Mathematics aims to deepen knowledge in the fields characteristic of Mathematics and develop competencies for formulating and solving complex mathematical problems referring to applications in different fields. The goal is to ensure complementary training characterized by a wide range of possibilities for deepening both theoretical aspects of Mathematics and its applications. The course provides the necessary competencies and knowledge to understand and formalize theoretical aspects in the fields of logic, algebra, geometry, foundations of Mathematics, and mathematical analysis, and to know and apply tools of mathematical statistics, mathematical physics, numerical analysis, and operations research. The path allows for deepening specific application aspects in various fields requiring the use of advanced mathematical tools, such as the study and modeling of complex systems, artificial intelligence and machine learning, data analysis, bioinformatics.
The structure of the training offer allows focusing preparation on both advanced theoretical and methodological aspects of Mathematics, and modeling aspects applicable in various disciplines (e.g., physics, computer science, biology, economics, engineering), contributing to scientific and technological progress. The planned training paths refer to the following learning areas.
Theoretical Mathematics Specific knowledge and competencies are provided regarding advanced aspects of Mathematics concerning logic, algebra, geometry, foundations of Mathematics, and mathematical analysis. The acquired knowledge and skills allow understanding the theory, formulating and proposing solutions to advanced mathematical problems, and following scientific evolution in the field. The training path is characterized by a certain degree of flexibility that allows deeper or less deep exploration of specific aspects of these Mathematics fields.
Applied Mathematics Specific knowledge and competencies are provided regarding advanced aspects of applied Mathematics concerning mathematical statistics, mathematical physics, numerical analysis, and operations research. The acquired knowledge and skills allow analyzing and proposing solutions to application problems requiring probabilistic or statistical modeling, description of physical phenomena, numerical modeling, and optimization. The flexibility of the training path allows defining different levels of deepening of these topics based on the chosen path.
Applications Competencies and abilities to apply mathematical models in specific application fields, such as information engineering, artificial intelligence and machine learning, analysis of biological data and bioinformatics, modeling of complex systems, data and time series analysis, discrete mathematics, graph theory. The path also provides the possibility to acquire competencies and methodologies for teaching Mathematics.
Thanks to their training, Master's graduates in Applied Mathematics will, depending on the case, be able to enter the workforce, using their specific competencies while valuing their mental flexibility and ability to collaborate with other experts, or continue their studies by participating in doctoral programs in Mathematics or related disciplines.
