High school diploma Tuition and fees For information on tuition and contribution amounts, visit the University website www.unisi.it/tasse Dates and deadlines For information on dates and deadlines, visit the University website "Study Plan" www.unisi.it/didattica/immatricolazioni-e-iscrizioni/immatricolazioni Roles Responsibilities for student mobility LEONARDO DISPERATI Student mobility coordinator ENRICO TAVARNELLI Chair/Chair of teaching committee Program, textbooks and objectives Professional title conferred by the degree.
Geological technician The main employment opportunities for graduates in Geological Sciences relate to public and private entities, companies and professional offices operating in applied geology for engineering, geological survey, hydrogeology, environmental geology, mineral and energy geology, territorial planning and soil protection. The graduate's preparation is suitable for continuing studies in the master's program in Class LM-74 (Geological Sciences and Technologies).
To practice the profession (DPR 328/01), it requires passing the State Exam and registration in Section B (Junior Geologist) of the Geologists' Register.
Final exam characteristics The final exam aims to verify the candidate's overall scientific maturity and communication skills through the preparation of a concise individual experimental, original or compilation report on one or more aspects of the studied disciplines; the exam consists of a public presentation and discussion before a committee.
The final exam preparation will be carried out by the student under the supervision of a supervisor, conducting autonomous activities at the University facilities or as an extracurricular internship at companies, design offices or consulting firms, companies, public bodies (Regions, Provinces, Municipal Technical Offices, ASL, museums, parks, etc.); this activity may involve acquiring field data through geological survey or environmental monitoring and processing, or it may be carried out through analysis of data obtained in technical/scientific laboratories, or it may constitute a critical re-elaboration of existing data in the literature.
Evaluation criteria will be the completeness and thoroughness of the report and the presentation ability. The final exam grade will be expressed in hundredths, with possible distinction; the merit score will primarily consider the quality of the entire study path undertaken by the student.
Required knowledge for admission To access the Geological Sciences L-34 degree course, it is necessary to hold a secondary school diploma or another foreign degree recognized as equivalent. Basic knowledge of mathematics, chemistry and physics is also required.
Additionally, English language knowledge at A2/2 level is required.
Initial student preparation is assessed through a test. Test results are used to determine any additional mandatory training requirements, to be fulfilled within the first year of the course.
The required knowledge for admission to the Geological Sciences degree course and the methods of their verification will be detailed in the Teaching Regulations, which will also indicate the additional mandatory training requirements if the verification is not positive.
Knowledge and understanding.
Generic Area The graduate in Geological Sciences will acquire:
• knowledge in geological disciplines, both basic and applied, framed within a broader context related to the environment and environmental sustainability;
• knowledge of the planet Earth and understanding of geological processes that led to the formation of rocks and sediments;
• knowledge of the geometric and compositional characteristics of rock bodies;
• knowledge of computer systems, mathematical methods, and statistical techniques for the analysis and processing of geological data;
• knowledge of global climate change and its consequences for the environment and humanity;
• knowledge of the environment and environmental sustainability as well as anthropology.
This objective will be achieved through the progressive addition of specific knowledge provided individually by teaching courses (through lectures, exercises, laboratories, and field trips) and critically discussed and linked together in cross-cutting activities such as seminars, multidisciplinary laboratories, and fieldwork.
Learning area: Scientific and methodological foundations The graduate in Geological Sciences will acquire knowledge and understanding related to:
mathematical methods and physical and chemical processes concerning Earth Sciences.
Learning area: Computer Science The graduate in Geological Sciences will acquire knowledge and understanding related to:
geodetic/cartographic reference systems;
georeferencing techniques using Geographic Information Systems (GIS);
collection of geological data using Global Positioning System (GPS);
techniques for analysis and processing of geological data.
Learning area: Earth Sciences Fundamentals The graduate in Geological Sciences will acquire knowledge and understanding related to:
internal structure of the Earth, plate tectonics, fragile and ductile structures of the Earth's crust;
erosive, transport, and accumulation processes, characteristic sediments of sedimentary environments, sedimentary structures, and principles of stratigraphy;
compact packing structures, crystal chemistry and crystal physics, mineral classification, techniques for mineral and rock investigation;
characteristics of major igneous, metamorphic, and sedimentary rocks;
fundamentals of taxonomy, evolutionary biology, biostratigraphy, paleoecology, paleobiogeography for Earth Sciences.
Learning area: Geological and Paleontological The graduate in Geological Sciences will acquire knowledge and understanding related to:
geological survey techniques, reading and interpretation of geological maps, reading and preparation of geological sections;
field activities in biostratigraphic, sedimentological, and structural contexts for the preparation of geological maps and sections;
anatomy and evolution of orogenic chains, geological history of the Alps and Apennines;
geological surfaces from subsurface and point data, geometric methods for constructing folds.
Learning area: Geomorphological and Applied Geology The graduate in Geological Sciences will acquire knowledge and understanding related to:
processes, factors, and conditions of Earth's landform modeling produced by physical and chemical alteration, types of landforms, time factor and climatic morphology;
stress, deformation, and failure of rocks and soils, physical and mechanical characteristics of soils, in-situ tests for soils;
water cycle and water balance, groundwater circulation under natural and forced conditions, water resources and their temporal variability;
basic optics and stereoscopic vision, aerial, terrestrial, and satellite imaging systems, geological-structural and lithological photointerpretation, multitemporal analysis;
geopedological and geoarchaeological investigations.
Learning area: Mineralogical, Petrographic and Geochemical The graduate in Geological Sciences will acquire knowledge and understanding related to:
petrogenetic processes and environments, classification and nomenclature of igneous, metamorphic, and sedimentary rocks, description and classification of rocks through chemical, diffractometric, spectroscopic analyses, and observations under polarized light and scanning electron microscope, main tectono-magmatic associations, metamorphic reactions, P-T regimes and P-T-t paths;
physical and chemical processes of mineral and rock weathering, geochemical characteristics of soil, atmospheric deposits, and surface and groundwater, sampling, preparation, and chemical analysis of geomaterial samples;
processes of magma formation, evolution, ascent, and emplacement, and physical-chemical and mineralogical characteristics of volcanic products;
solid state structures and relationships between structure and physical-chemical properties of natural and synthetic solids;
environmental impact of sulfide mineralization exploitation in southern Tuscany;
petrographic applications for the analysis of historical buildings and archaeological artifacts.
Learning area: Geophysics The graduate in Geological Sciences will acquire knowledge and understanding related to:
concepts and methodologies of geophysical surveys, seismology, seismic hazard estimation, gravimetry.

SECTION: Judgment autonomy
URL: https://unisi.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/10894

Judgment autonomy.
The graduate will acquire the ability to: independently assess the complexity of natural systems, plan geological surveys, collect and process necessary data while evaluating its quality and reliability; assess the role and responsibilities of Earth Sciences in managing and protecting territory, with reference to geological hazards, safeguarding and utilization of raw materials (water, soil, subsurface), environmental resources in terrestrial and marine contexts, and conservation of stone cultural heritage.
This objective is primarily achieved through courses in the 2nd and 3rd years of study, focusing on characteristic and complex aspects of Earth Sciences, whose understanding requires an integrated reading of various data types (bibliographic, analytical, cartographic) not exclusively geological, and involves independently compiling final reports on experiences. Further judgment autonomy is finally acquired through the completion of the thesis on a specific topic of interest to the student. The acquisition of judgment autonomy is verified through evaluation of performance in courses referring to characteristic disciplinary sectors, the degree of autonomy and work capacity, also in group settings, expressed in written reports on experiential activities, the final exam, and the internship.

Learning capacity.
The graduate will independently learn through the use of advanced texts, databases, and online information to continuously deepen and update their knowledge. The achievement of this objective is guaranteed by the extensive availability of bibliographic and computer tools at the teaching site, easily accessible to students (libraries, computer networks, etc.).
The objective is verified through the combination of various exam assessments, reports, seminars, and the graduation thesis accompanying the student's career.

Ability to apply knowledge and understanding.
Generic Area The graduate in Geological Sciences will acquire the ability to:
• apply acquired knowledge to the analysis and description of geomaterials in the laboratory and in the field, as well as to the study of geological processes and environmental issues using modern tools and applying quantitative methods with a professional approach;
• use computer tools, mathematical methods, and statistical techniques for the analysis and processing of geological data.
This objective will be achieved through specific courses and laboratory and field experiences, leading the student to analyze, describe, and critically discuss a geological process or environmental issue.

Learning Area: Scientific and Methodological Foundations The graduate in Geological Sciences will be able to:
apply mathematical methods to model and analyze geological processes and phenomena;
interpret physical and chemical processes in geological phenomena and define the laws governing them.

Learning Area: Computer Science The graduate in Geological Sciences will be able to:
apply georeferencing techniques to Earth Sciences;
use GPS for geological data collection;
apply techniques for analysis and processing of geological data.

Learning Area: Earth Sciences Fundamentals The graduate in Geological Sciences will be able to:
recognize common mega and mesostructures of the Earth's crust;
recognize characteristic sediments of sedimentary environments and major sedimentary structures;
describe compact packing structures and use main techniques for mineralogical and petrographic investigation, crystal chemical and crystal physical characterization of minerals;
recognize major igneous, metamorphic, and sedimentary rocks;
recognize common fossil remains and traces and their associated sedimentary paleoenvironments.

Learning Area: Geological and Paleontological The graduate in Geological Sciences will be able to:
conduct geological surveys and produce geological maps and sections in igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic contexts;
perform biostratigraphic, sedimentological, and structural observations for the production of geological maps and sections;
analyze the evolution of orogenic systems and fundamental processes in the development and evolution of the Alpine and Apennine chains;
reconstruct geological surfaces from subsurface and point data.

Learning Area: Geomorphological and Applied Geology The graduate in Geological Sciences will be able to:
describe processes, factors, and conditions of Earth's modeling;
recognize major forms and deposits associated with modeling agents;
analyze stresses, deformations, and rock and soil fractures, characterize soils from a physical-mechanical perspective;
evaluate hydroclimatic parameters related to the water cycle, characterize aquifers from a physical and hydrodynamic perspective, quantitatively assess groundwater resources at watershed and aquifer scale;
extract geological and geotopic information from aerial and terrestrial photogrammetry and develop additional methods for producing spatial data containing derived information also with multitemporal characteristics;
plan surveys for soil protection and safeguarding of archaeological sites of interest.

Learning Area: Mineralogical, Petrological and Geochemical The graduate in Geological Sciences will be able to:
characterize rocks from a chemical, mineralogical, and petrographic perspective through chemical, diffractometric, spectroscopic analyses, and observations in polarized light and scanning electron microscopy;
describe processes and environments of petrogenesis, metamorphic reactions, P-T regimes, and P-T-t paths;
identify main factors and processes regulating the abundance, distribution, and behavior of chemical elements in the surface environment (air, soil, water);
analyze the relationship between structure and physical-chemical properties of natural and synthetic solids;
define the physical-chemical and mineralogical characteristics of volcanic products and the processes of magma formation and emplacement;
assess the environmental impact of sulfide mineralization exploitation;
use petrographic methods and applications for the analysis of historical buildings and archaeological artifacts.

Learning Area: Geophysics The graduate in Geological Sciences will be able to:
describe basic physical concepts for the study of the Earth and the main geophysical investigation techniques for subsurface characterization.

Communication Skills.
The graduate will have the ability to communicate information, ideas, problems, and solutions related to Earth Sciences correctly in their native language, both orally and in writing, to both specialist and non-specialist audiences. Ability to use technical language in a second European language other than Italian, with particular reference to English. Familiarity with the use of major computer tools and network resources useful for acquiring and disseminating information. The objective is achieved progressively throughout the university career, through encouraged collective discussion during laboratories, field experiences, and seminars held during the three-year program. Finally, the preparation and presentation of the thesis (in terms of completeness, clarity, and interest) allows the student to test their communication ability. This thus becomes the final element for verifying communication aptitude.
Expected occupational and professional opportunities for graduates.
Geological Technician The predominant occupational opportunities, related to the figure of the graduate in Geological Sciences, are to be referred to public and private entities, companies, and professional offices operating in applied geology for engineering, geological surveying, hydrogeology, environmental geology, mining and energy geology, territorial planning, and soil protection. The graduate's preparation is relevant for continuing studies in the master's program in Class LM-74 (Geological Sciences and Technologies). For the exercise of the profession (DPR 328/01), this exists upon passing the State Exam and registration in Section B (Junior Geologist) of the Register of Geologists.
Official teaching and assessment languages.
ITALIANO Associated competencies for the function.
Geological Technician The graduate in Geological Sciences has acquired basic and fundamental knowledge for understanding and characterizing a territory geologically, as well as the methods to support specific investigations regarding planning and its management, even in quantitative terms. Specific abilities include laboratory experiments and autonomy in conducting field activities (particularly geological surveying and the concurrent collection of samples and various types of data) and in drafting structured and complete technical reports.
Function in the workplace context.
Geological Technician The geological technician operates in the field of geological and basic, regional, and national technical cartography; carries out support activities for data acquisition for the prevention of geological-environmental risks; conducts basic tests and monitoring aimed at research, evaluation, and safeguarding of water resources and aquifer remediation; performs laboratory tests for characterizing rocks and soils; conducts sampling and on-site tests on land and at sea, assists in the execution of basic geophysical surveys; supports research and development of natural raw materials, particularly in the oil industry; collects geological data for environmental impact assessment, aimed at extraction activities and the recovery of abandoned sites; is involved in the recovery of secondary raw materials; develops research, use, and commercialization of ornamental stone materials; assists construction sites, mining plants, and processing facilities; supports research, valorization, and protection of cultural heritage.
In the workplace context, collaborations can be developed with other professional technical figures, identifiable among engineers, architects, chemists, biologists, and archaeologists. To express the aforementioned functions in the private professional context, it is necessary to pass the State Exam and then register in Section B (Junior Geologist) of the Register of Geologists.
Description of specific educational objectives.
The Course of Study in Geological Sciences trains graduates in Class L-34, who, placing themselves within the European references for the field of Earth Sciences, acquire basic knowledge of geology and geological processes that characterize the planet and are therefore capable of promoting a conscious and sustainable use of Earth's resources. The graduate will thus be able to frame geological processes within the correct spatial-temporal context, as well as recognize the role of Earth Sciences in society and their responsibilities in research and management of resources, respecting the environment. The course prepares the graduate specifically by prioritizing practical field and laboratory/exercise activities, respecting the figure of a geologist who prefers direct contact with the specificities and typical problems of a territory. To achieve these objectives, the course offers a valorization of basic knowledge and understanding of mathematical, physical, chemical, and computer science disciplines (from MAT/01 to MAT/09, SECS-S/06, from FIS/01 to FIS/08, INF/01, ING-INF/05, from CHIM/01 to CHIM/03, CHIM/06, and CHIM/12), including principles of digital cartography, as well as teachings on Earth Science disciplines from GEO/01 to GEO/09, which are then also taken up at the level of course characterization throughout their entire spectrum from GEO/01 to GEO/12. For the identification and better management of application issues, which may relate to the junior geologist profession and their connection with cross-cutting or management skills, affinity or integrative activities are mainly dedicated to Pedology, Ecology, Anthropology, Physical Chemistry and Environmental and Cultural Heritage Chemistry, and Experimental and Applied Physics (AGR/14, BIO/07, BIO/08, CHIM/02, CHIM/12, FIS/01, and FIS/07). For information and training on safety in laboratory and field activities, a dedicated activity on workplace safety with specific reference to the geological environment is provided. Additionally, there is an obligation for external/internal activities in the form of training internships preferably at companies, public structures, and laboratories. There are also Erasmus agreements for study stays at other European or extra-European universities. For the above, the training path will be structured with: - Frontal lectures aimed at providing fundamental knowledge in various fields of Earth Sciences and in specific application sectors, proper to the professional field of the junior geologist; - Field experiences, present also in the first year but concentrated in the second and third years, aimed at understanding geological phenomena in their real manifestations, studying and describing the geometry of rock bodies, characterizing them functionally for various application purposes, and learning basic cartographic and geological surveying techniques; - Laboratory experiences, present in all three years but concentrated in the third year, dedicated to modern experimental, analytical methods, and data processing for the production of geological maps.
To individually follow the student's career (helping them focus their educational goals, overcome difficulties, and plan their studies), some faculty members of the course take on the role of tutors.

Final Exam Characteristics The degree is obtained by passing a final exam consisting of the evaluation by the graduation committee of the final thesis written by the student under the supervision of a faculty advisor. The final thesis consists of a brief written work, supported by appropriate bibliographic references, on a theoretical or empirical topic chosen by the student according to the procedures defined by the final exam regulation established by the competent academic body. To pass the final exam, the student must demonstrate having acquired, in addition to adequate knowledge and understanding of the chosen topic, autonomous learning and research capabilities; the ability to correctly use the consulted literature and necessary data sources; and the ability to present and defend scientific arguments logically and coherently. The final thesis may be written in English; it must be written in English if students graduate in a study path conducted in English. The final exam is worth 3 CFU. The score for the final exam is expressed on a scale of 100. The graduation committee assigns a score for the final exam that takes into account the average score in hundredths from the examination results, increased by any additional points specified in the final exam regulation for specific academic merits, and the quality of the written thesis. If the overall evaluation exceeds 110/110, the committee may award honors unanimously.
Prerequisites for Admission To be admitted to the Bachelor's Degree program, one must hold a secondary school diploma or another foreign degree recognized as equivalent. The required knowledge for admission is that acquired at the secondary school level, with particular reference to mathematics, along with a basic general culture. The specific mathematical knowledge required for admission will be specified in the course's academic regulations. Additionally, English language knowledge at least at level A2/2 (CEFR) is required. The course's academic regulations will specify the methods for assessing this knowledge, which may include more stringent requirements for English-taught pathways.
The assessment of the student's initial preparation will be conducted according to the criteria and methods detailed in the course's academic regulations. It will be based on a test, developed and administered nationally, designed to assess aptitude and minimum preparation required to undertake economic studies, through verbal comprehension, basic mathematical knowledge, and simple logical problems. The assessment of English language knowledge will be conducted through tests organized in collaboration with the University of Siena Language Center. The course's academic regulations will specify any additional educational requirements in case of a negative assessment of the admission test and the English language test; these requirements must be fulfilled in the first year of study, possibly through specific recovery courses in mathematics and English organized by the relevant departments.
Degree Awarded.
Bachelor's Degree (First Level) in Economic and Banking Sciences Teaching Delivery Method Conventional Knowledge and Understanding.
Generic Area Referring to the business context, the graduate in Economic and Banking Sciences knows and understands the role and functioning of capital markets in the allocation of financial resources. In this context, they know and understand the structure and functioning of financial markets, financial intermediaries, and the essential characteristics of financial instruments and products. They know and understand the main differences between insurance intermediaries, securities intermediaries, and credit intermediaries, with particular attention to the types of risks assumed. They know and understand the functions and characteristics of bond, equity, and derivative instruments, also from a portfolio perspective.
Regarding the economic context, the graduate in Economic and Banking Sciences possesses a good understanding of major economic models, both microeconomic and macroeconomic, and the determinants of key economic variables (GDP, inflation rate, exchange rate), and is able to understand and interpret the economic framework, conduct market condition analysis for the enterprise, and develop a consequent business strategy.
Regarding the legal context, the graduate in Economic and Banking Sciences knows and understands legal terminology; masters the main institutions of private and public law and the principles related to the legal regulation of sole and collective enterprises.
Specifically regarding the quantitative context, the graduate in Economic and Banking Sciences knows the mathematical tools useful for economic decision-making; masters basic statistical tools, understanding their use in descriptive and inferential contexts. They know the mathematical tools for analyzing interest rates, annuities, and amortization.
The graduate in Economic and Banking Sciences has a good knowledge of the English language and the ability to understand written and spoken English.
They know the main computer tools useful for economic and business analysis.
These knowledge and understanding capabilities must be acquired and verified primarily through curricular courses and their respective examination results across different areas.
Business Area The graduate in Economic and Banking Sciences possesses a good command of the theory and techniques of business management, and the theory and techniques of preparing a business balance sheet, whether for a private or public enterprise. They have a good knowledge of national accounting principles (OIC) and (depending on the chosen courses) a good knowledge of international accounting principles (IFRS); they know analytical accounting and are able to understand its results in terms of costs, revenues, and operational margins for specific business segments.
Depending on the curriculum, the graduate acquires basic knowledge of corporate finance and the tools to analyze and understand corporate financial decisions.
The graduate in Economic and Banking Sciences knows and understands the role and functioning of capital markets in the allocation of financial resources. In this context, they know and understand the structure and functioning of financial markets, financial intermediaries, and the essential characteristics of financial instruments and products. They know and understand the main differences between insurance intermediaries, securities intermediaries, and credit intermediaries, with particular attention to the types of risks assumed. They know and understand the functions and characteristics of bond, equity, and derivative instruments, also from a portfolio perspective.
The graduate in Economic and Banking Sciences, among financial intermediaries, knows and is able to understand the specifics of banks, their role in payment systems, savings allocation, and savings management. They know the different types of banking operations. They have a good knowledge of bank management balances, with particular reference to risk management. They have a good knowledge of the banking balance sheet and the determinants of bank performance.
Economic Area The graduate in Economic and Banking Sciences possesses a good understanding of the historical evolution of the economy and is able to comprehend how economic variables have influenced the decisions of economic operators over time.
The graduate in Economic and Banking Sciences possesses a good understanding of major economic models, both microeconomic and macroeconomic, and the determinants of key economic variables (GDP, inflation rate, exchange rate), and is able to understand and interpret the economic framework, conduct market condition analysis for the enterprise, and develop a consequent business strategy.
Depending on the curriculum and chosen courses, the graduate in Economic and Banking Sciences possesses:
a) a rigorous basic knowledge of econometric theory and main quantitative methods, enabling them to set up, process, and evaluate a basic empirical project, including learning the functionalities and use of the econometric package STATA;
b) knowledge of the functioning and policies of the labor market, both in Italy and Europe, based on the analysis of key topics according to the most recent theories and models;
c) knowledge of issues concerning externalities and public goods/environmental goods, including the analysis of policy instruments proposed by economic theory (command-and-control instruments and market-based instruments such as taxes, subsidies, and tradable permits);
d) knowledge of the theoretical and empirical foundations of imperfect markets (monopoly, oligopoly, monopolistic competition), including the analysis of competition/collusion levels with reference to variables such as market power, price discrimination, vertical relations, product differentiation, advertising, research and development, and also considering anti-trust policies and forms and models of regulation.
Legal Area The graduate in Economic and Banking Sciences knows and understands legal terminology; knows the main institutions of private law (rights of persons, property rights, obligations and their sources) and public law (the Italian Constitution and the Italian state political organization with references to the European framework).
The graduate in Economic and Banking Sciences knows the principles related to the legal regulation of sole and collective enterprises, with particular attention to the practical and applied aspects of the studied institutions, and (depending on the chosen curriculum) has a comprehensive knowledge of harmonized European legislation regarding business and company law.
Depending on the curriculum and chosen courses, the graduate knows and understands the foundations of domestic and community special legislation regarding banking, financial, and insurance enterprises, and in particular has a thorough understanding of the institutional mechanisms underlying the banking regulatory framework, the specificities of banks (and the products offered), and the supervision mechanisms (national and community) applicable to them. The graduate understands the legal system currently governing individual and collective labor relations, paying attention also to the historical evolution of the discipline and labor market dynamics. Finally, the graduate, through the analysis of the main institutions characterizing administration from the perspective of its organization, activities, and relations with other subjects of the legal order, acquires the necessary tools to understand the principles and rules governing public and private subjects (under certain profiles) equated to public entities.
Mathematical-Statistical Area The graduate in Economic and Banking Sciences has a good knowledge and understanding of the basic tools of mathematical analysis and linear algebra necessary for statistical, economic, financial, and social analyses. Additionally, they know the tools of probability calculus and the main methods of descriptive and inferential statistics; in particular, the graduate has knowledge aimed at data collection, analysis, synthesis, and interpretation of economic, business, and financial data.
The graduate in Economic and Banking Sciences knows and understands mathematical techniques for analyzing interest rates, annuities, and amortization. They have a good command of the fundamental elements for the quantitative study of profiles related to financial instruments.
Finally, depending on the curriculum and chosen courses, the graduate in Economic and Banking Sciences possesses a rigorous basic education in econometric theory, with particular reference to the multiple regression model, and a good knowledge of statistical methods for multivariate data analysis.

Critical judgment.
At the end of the course, graduates in Economic and Banking Sciences will:
- demonstrate a critical approach and reflection on how data analysis and model usage can be exploited for descriptive or operational purposes;
- show full awareness of the importance of addressing and solving problems related to choosing between different financing, investment, and risk coverage opportunities; simultaneously identifying the financial consequences of each decision;
- be aware of the economic, social, and political impacts of financial decisions, formulating their own opinions on the matter.
- be able to access statistical sources relevant to their field of study, as well as acquire data through field surveys, analyze it critically, and interpret it.
These abilities will be achieved and verified by cultivating through critical discussion with professors the student's ability to express and discuss their viewpoint in class.
Learning ability.
At the end of the training path, graduates in Economic and Banking Sciences will:
- demonstrate evident improvement in the ability to exploit available information to analyze and solve economic-business problems;
- demonstrate greater predisposition to profit from acquired knowledge;
- have acquired mastery of the knowledge necessary to continue studies in the field of financial economics.
This ability will be achieved by the student through regular study habits and will be verified through support activities for exam preparation and the final thesis.
Ability to apply knowledge and understanding.
Generic Area Through knowledge of accounting techniques and financial statement preparation, the graduate in Economic and Banking Sciences is able to manage corporate accounting, critically analyzing the flow of data on costs and revenues and identifying potential issues. Additionally, they are able to calculate the product cost for the company and organize and manage internal auditing processes. The graduate in Economic and Banking Sciences is able to prepare and analyze the corporate financial statement of a national company and analyze a financial statement prepared according to international standards. They will be able to monitor the economic, financial, and equity conditions of the company.
Through knowledge of the functioning mechanisms of the macroeconomic and microeconomic market, and other acquired economic knowledge, the graduate in Economic and Banking Sciences is able to conduct a critical analysis of the economic cycle and its effects on consumer and business choices; capable of analyzing the reference market and developing the optimal strategy for the company, both in the short and long term.
Through knowledge acquired in the legal field, the graduate in Economic and Banking Sciences is able to critically manage the legal constraints of the company, with particular attention to contracts the company must handle, and analyze the effects that changes in national, and depending on the curriculum, European and international regulations may have on the company's short and long-term choices.
The graduate in Economic and Banking Sciences, thanks to knowledge acquired in the quantitative field, is able to apply mathematical-statistical models to the analysis of micro and macroeconomic data, having the ability to use these tools to obtain statistically robust indicators of the company's situation and to make reliable forecasts of the future trends of relevant variables for the company.
The graduate in Economic and Banking Sciences is able to communicate in English and integrate effectively into an international work group.
They will be able to creatively use the most important computer programs useful for business and economic analysis.
The ability to apply knowledge and understanding will be acquired through curricular courses, seminar activities, also in English, involving experts from the business world, and participation in training experiences aimed at acquiring soft skills.
The writing of the thesis represents an important opportunity for students to apply the acquired knowledge.
The ability to apply knowledge and understanding is primarily verified through passing exams and the evaluation of the thesis.
Business Area Through knowledge of accounting techniques and financial statement preparation, the graduate is able to manage corporate accounting, critically analyzing the flow of data on costs and revenues and identifying potential issues. Additionally, they are able to calculate the product cost for the company and organize and manage internal auditing processes. The graduate in Economic and Banking Sciences is able to prepare and analyze the corporate financial statement of a national company and analyze a financial statement prepared according to international standards. They will be able to monitor the economic, financial, and equity conditions of the company.
Depending on the chosen curriculum, the graduate in Economic and Banking Sciences is able to, at a basic level, assess the impact of corporate financial decisions on value creation for shareholders.
The graduate in Economic and Banking Sciences is capable of critically analyzing the differences between capital markets with varying degrees of orientation towards intermediaries and markets, interpreting the consequences on the development model of different geographical areas and the trends of the European capital market.
They are able to recognize different business models of financial companies, evaluating their risks and performance, also in relation to the economic and regulatory context. They are able to critically interpret financial instrument innovation, recognizing the role each instrument plays in meeting the needs of issuers and investors. They are able, at a basic level, to manage a portfolio of financial instruments, measuring expected risks and performance.
The graduate in Economic and Banking Sciences is able to compare and evaluate different banking business models, interpret the collection and lending policies implemented by different banking companies. They are able, at a basic level, to conduct a creditworthiness assessment. They are capable of understanding the contractual structures of collection and investment operations, evaluating risks and costs for the involved parties. They are capable of critically analyzing the structure of the banking balance sheet, in terms of equity and economic equilibria, comparing different companies. They are able to interpret in essential terms the evolution of the banking industry in the face of technological challenges. They are able to assess, at a basic level, the impact of regulation, costs, and expected benefits.
Economic Area Thanks to acquired knowledge, the graduate in Economic and Banking Sciences is able to conduct a critical analysis of major historical-economic phenomena as a guide to understanding current economic evolution.
Through knowledge of the functioning mechanisms of the macroeconomic market, the graduate in Economic and Banking Sciences is capable of conducting a critical analysis of the economic cycle and its effects on consumer and business choices.
Due to knowledge of microeconomic market functioning and analysis of business decisions in various market forms, the graduate in Economic and Banking Sciences is able to analyze the reference market for the company and develop the optimal strategy for the company both in the short and long term.
As a result of knowledge of econometric, industrial economics, environmental economic policy, and labor economics models, depending on the curriculum and chosen courses, the graduate in Economic and Banking Sciences is able to organize their own dataset, specify estimation equations, and statistically test hypotheses suggested by economic theory, understand the different constraints imposed by market forms and strategic interdependence with other companies operating in the same sector, address the problem of efficient and sustainable resource use over time, understand the functioning of the labor market and intervene in the debate on related policies, acquiring some of the specific competencies of a human resources manager, labor market analyst, or labor consultant.
Legal Area The graduate in Economic and Banking Sciences is able to critically manage the legal constraints of the company, with particular attention to contracts the company must enter into with suppliers and customers.
The graduate in Economic and Banking Sciences is able to analyze the effects that national regulations, and depending on the curriculum, European and international regulations, both common and special law (banking, financial, and insurance), may have on the company's short and long-term choices.
Depending on the curriculum and chosen courses, the graduate is able to apply national and European banking, insurance, and financial regulations to concrete cases, recognizing their peculiarities compared to common company law. They are also able to manage the framework of principles and rules to which public and private subjects (under certain profiles) are subject. Finally, they are able to manage legal relationships with employees and legal issues arising from the company's international expansion.
Mathematical-Statistical Area The graduate in Economic and Banking Sciences is able to apply mathematical tools and statistical techniques to the analysis of microeconomic and macroeconomic data and the study of corporate data flows. In particular, from corporate data, the graduate is able to evaluate company performance, identify costs and benefits based on possible choices, analyze consumer demand structure, and critically assess strategic growth or consolidation hypotheses.
The graduate is able to perform the main quantitative evaluations of financial and credit instruments, critically compare market prices of bonds, and clearly articulate a financial valuation or decision problem.
Finally, depending on the curriculum and chosen courses, the graduate in Economic and Banking Sciences is able to estimate a multivariate regression model and apply the most important multivariate techniques to complex data systems and interpret the results.

Communication Skills.
Graduates in Economic and Banking Sciences will also be able to:

- demonstrate solid written communication skills, also showing autonomy in the critical revision of their own work.
These skills will be acquired and verified through training in interviews and written assessments, as well as through language courses.

Administrative personnel. Financial and insurance consultants. Economic and financial analyst. Economic and market analysis within research, analysis, planning, and control departments of financial institutions, companies, and public and private entities.

Accounting expert. Self-employment.

- research bodies conducting statistical-environmental research,
- banks and insurance companies,
- pharmaceutical companies,
- all industrial sectors managing production lines, market research, and statistical quality control,
- bodies dealing with territorial analysis in environmental, geological, physical, etc. contexts.

Description of admission tests.
It will be based on a test, developed and conducted nationally, aimed at assessing the necessary aptitude and minimum preparation required to undertake economic studies, through tests of verbal comprehension, basic mathematical knowledge, and simple logical reasoning problems. The assessment of English language knowledge will be carried out through tests conducted in collaboration with the University of Siena Language Center. The test is orienting and establishes any additional educational obligations in case of negative assessment of the access test and the English language knowledge test, possibly in the form of specific recovery courses in mathematics and English.
Workplace function.
Operational staff in banking and insurance intermediaries. Economic and financial analyst. Graduates in Economic and Banking Sciences can perform support roles in research, analysis, and consultancy in economic and financial fields. Graduates will be able to understand texts, research topics, and methodological approaches typical of economics; analyze market and business economic processes and financial processes in their mutual interconnection and within the broader context of social phenomena; identify and address the economic, financial, social, and environmental implications of different economic policy options; propose well-substantiated effective and efficient solutions to complex economic/social problems; apply main quantitative methods to economic, social, and financial phenomena.
Accounting expert. Analysis of company, professional, and private subject accounting. Analysis of tax and fiscal regulations. Analysis of labor law regulations. Analysis of the economic framework.
Statistical and data processing expert. Graduates in Economic and Banking Sciences who have chosen a curriculum with a significant focus on statistical training and data analysis will be able to assume operational and specialized responsibilities in collecting, analyzing, and interpreting numerical data to facilitate understanding of reality and provide objective tools to aid decision-making processes by governing bodies, companies, etc.

https://scienze-economiche-bancarie.unisi.it/it Specific educational objectives description.
The Bachelor's degree in Economic and Banking Sciences aims, with levels of depth consistent with the chosen path, to train graduates with:
- solid knowledge of financial intermediary processes in business, economic, legal, and statistical-quantitative aspects, related to professional opportunities in the banking, financial, and insurance sectors.
- economic knowledge related to professional opportunities in economic analysis in companies, financial institutions, and public and private entities.
- knowledge of the main statistical-quantitative methods applied to economic, social, and financial phenomena, related to professional opportunities in statistical analysis in companies, financial institutions, and public and private entities.
To account for the different training needs required today for the various professional outcomes of graduates in Economic and Banking Sciences, the Bachelor's degree may be structured into curricula, aimed at specifically deepening the different profiles in which the training is structured, while maintaining a solid and broad common base.
The structure of the study path and its articulation, depending on the different orientations available to the student, are defined as follows. The study path is characterized by significant emphasis on:
i- financial intermediaries economics and financial mathematics (SSD SECS-P/11 and SECS-S/06);
ii- economic disciplines (SSD SECS-P/01-2-3-5).
Students can orient their path towards a plurality of profiles.
If the orientation is to acquire greater knowledge of banking and insurance company products, services, and management criteria and the institutional context in which they operate, students can deepen business disciplines both in financial intermediaries economics (SECS-P/11) and in the field of corporate finance (SECS-P/09) and/or legal disciplines (IUS/04, IUS/05, IUS/07, IUS/10).
If the orientation is to deepen knowledge of the economic-financial context from a more strictly economic perspective, also considering variables of economic policy and environmental and social implications, students can expand the space reserved in their study path for disciplines of SSD SECS-P/01, SECS-P/02, SECS-P/03, SECS-P/04, and SECS-P/05.
Finally, if the orientation is to deepen knowledge of quantitative methods used for economic and social analysis and applications to finance, students can expand the space reserved for disciplines of SSD SECS-S/01, SECS-S/03, SECS-S/04, SECS-S/05.
In the linguistic field, in addition to a minimum mandatory base in English (preparatory level to B2 of the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages), higher levels of training (in English and/or a second European Union language) may be provided for students with better competencies at entry and/or within a curriculum taught in English.
Finally, graduates acquire competencies:
- in the computer science area, also with specific applications to the financial area,
or, alternatively at their choice,
- derived from internship and training experiences.

(3) Communication and marketing offices of companies or organizations Final Exam Characteristics The completion of the educational path requires a final exam consisting of a written work produced independently by the student. The objective of the final exam is: to verify and assess skills in identifying and sourcing information, methodological skills, mastery of available scientific literature on the topic, critical abilities, and the ability to adhere to scientific communication norms.
One or more professors guide the student in preparing the exam (research question, appropriate methodology, formal appropriateness, adequate content, bibliographic selection, formal and ethical correctness). The exam format is agreed upon with the professor. It can be conducted in Italian or English upon request to the Teaching Committee.
The final exam can be a written work/thesis or another format proposed by the professor according to the methodology most suitable for the chosen discipline.
For the range of final exam formats, evaluation criteria, merit scores, and the procedure for assigning a tutor for the final exam, refer to the Course Regulations.
Required Knowledge for Access Those who possess a secondary school diploma of the second level or another foreign qualification recognized as equivalent may access the degree course.
To be admitted to the degree course, students must demonstrate possession of skills in the following knowledge areas:
- General culture,
- Italian language,
- Logic,
- Computer science.
Verification is conducted through a test; failure to pass the test does not prevent enrollment in the Degree Course but requires recovery of academic debts through a personalized path.
Students must possess English language knowledge at least at A2 level. Verification of competence is carried out through a diagnostic test of communicative competence level in English (computerized test) or recognition of existing certifications (IELTS or CAMBRIDGE ESOL).
Awarded Degree.
COMMUNICATION SCIENCES Knowledge and Understanding.
Communication Learning Area Basic knowledge is specific to the foundational disciplines of Communication Sciences (L-LIN/01, M-STO/04, SPS/04, SPS/08, L-FIL-LET/12, M-FIL/05); in particular, sociolinguistic (L-FIL-LET/12), semiotic (M-FIL/05), anthropological disciplines (M-DEA/01), with particular reference to philosophical-theoretical (M-FIL/01), psychological (M-PSI/01), and legal disciplines in the communication context (IUS/01). The Communication Learning Area complements the basic critical knowledge with advanced knowledge in the communication sector. Throughout the educational path, the main forms and types of communication are examined, each corresponding to one or more professional sectors. Around this framework of characteristic disciplines, students can draw on a selection of relevant and related disciplines in various ways and from different perspectives within the following disciplinary strands: Linguistic-Cognitive Disciplines, Historical-Social Disciplines, Social Communication Languages, and Communication Techniques. The educational path is relevant and integrable for choosing master's degrees, and the selection of courses corresponding to three different professional streams: Mass Communication (SPS/03, SPS/07, SPS/08, SPS/09, M-STO/04, MPSI/01, L-LIN/01); Communication Technologies (ING-INF/05, L-ART/06, M-GGR/01, M-PSI/01, ICAR/13); Business Communication (SECS-P/02, SECS-P/08, SPS/08, SECS-S/01). At the end of the path, graduates will have acquired basic knowledge of language description levels (phonological, morphosyntactic, lexical, discursive, pragmatic); knowledge of theoretical models and conceptual frameworks for analyzing contemporary society; Basic knowledge of communication principles; Knowledge of text analysis methodologies regarding content, message, expressive capacity, and communicative effectiveness of the text; Knowledge of the social, economic, historical role of media and communication technologies; Knowledge of technical resources for developing messages and content in production processes.

Autonomy of judgment.
Graduates must be able to exercise the ability to quickly search for and obtain all necessary data and information to deepen their knowledge of the various communication and cultural processes occurring in society, both in their theoretical formulations and regarding their implications in different contexts and themes;
they must therefore have also acquired skills and abilities in identifying and retrieving sources from which to extract the aforementioned information, both national and international in origin;
they must also possess the ability to select the most effective research practices and methodologies for analyzing and deepening specific research topics and/or questions, with reference to the most recent trends in the various sectors of communication sciences;
Graduates must finally demonstrate the ability to operate in an interdisciplinary perspective: that is, to identify in the disciplines and study areas addressed during the degree course, problems and methods that, while not immediately relevant to communication processes, allow adopting innovative and alternative viewpoints regarding the social and cultural phenomena considered.
Autonomy of judgment is acquired both during the preparation of the final thesis and through participation in lectures, as well as during seminar and exercise activities. Graduates must demonstrate during the training process the ability to transform acquired knowledge into an autonomous capacity for analyzing the theoretical-critical debate, documentation problems, and methodology. This ability is verified through: final exams and written and oral intermediate assessment tests, reports and elaborations resulting from seminar and workshop activities, and the final assessment test.
Capacity for learning.
To be able to undertake subsequent studies with a high degree of autonomy, graduates must:
- develop the ability to learn both the content and the scientific terminology that identifies each disciplinary field or research area covered by the educational offer;
- learn to use synergistically the different sources through which educational content is delivered (lectures, seminars, study texts, handouts, etc.);
- learn to focus on their specific knowledge interests and select didactic and training activities according to these (referring both to course selection, where this option is available, and to the selection of topics they wish to deepen within each course and for the purpose of writing the thesis).
Graduates must demonstrate having achieved an adequate understanding and sufficient critical sense in studying scientific literature and having developed a good level of autonomy in choosing future training paths (master's degree, master's programs). Writing ability and, in general, expressive mastery are fundamental criteria for assessment in final exams and written and oral assessment tests, as well as in the final assessment test. However, the most important aspect is verifying the ability to select and hierarchize topics of a discipline or problem. Each degree course exam (and particularly the final dissertation) represents a moment of verification of these abilities. These are supplemented by written and/or oral intermediate tests conducted during courses. All these opportunities serve to interactively verify (also in the presence of all students) the state of knowledge achieved by each participant, enabling them to understand areas for improvement and potential delays in preparation, but also to know and deepen, in a way that is not merely remunerative (in terms of final grade), their personal inclinations.
Capacity to apply knowledge and understanding.
Area of learning in communication
- Skills necessary for producing effective communication, in written and oral form, with particular reference to digital technologies (ING-INF/05, M-PSI/01, SPS/08);
- skills related to the use of main tools for archiving, processing, managing, and disseminating information, with particular reference to digital technologies (ING-INF/05, M-PSI/01);
- adequate knowledge of the scientific terminology used in each studied discipline and of the specialized languages typical of professional sectors to which they are directly relevant.
At the end of the course, graduates will have acquired: the ability to apply theoretical models and conceptual frameworks to the analysis of contemporary society; the ability to analyze the social, economic, historical role of media and communication technologies; the ability to evaluate the social and cultural impact of mediated discourse;
the ability to use technical resources for developing messages and content in production processes and to develop content for various areas (business, institutional, public relations) and to apply the basic principles of communication; the ability to analyze discourse in various types of media; the ability to apply content analysis methodologies. Graduates will have the necessary skills for socializing and presenting the sectoral information and knowledge acquired during their studies, as well as for presenting and enhancing the results (creative, analytical, project-based) they have achieved; whether in written or oral presentations, graduates will be able to operate in different communication situations, varying registers and codes in relation to interlocutors and the purpose of the communication process; they must also demonstrate the ability to use graphic, media, and computer support; in the case of technologically mediated communication, graduates must be able to select the most suitable means to reach a specific audience and demonstrate the ability to adapt communication content and form to the technological and cultural characteristics of the medium in question. In addition to acquiring skills related to the communication/presentation/dissemination of information, problems, and ideas in an individual form, graduates must have developed the ability to organize and manage complex communication processes involving multiple subjects. Graduates will have developed their communication skills through: intermediate exercises, seminar and workshop activities.
In each of these settings, continuous exchange with teachers and fellow students occurs. The final thesis corresponds to the ability to communicate all phases of a project, from its conception to final consumption, using available documentation and scientific literature, with language accessible to both professionals and a broader audience. The acquisition of advanced English communication skills will enable graduates to transmit competencies and information, identify and solve problems in English. Advanced English communication competence as a tool for communication in all competencies (production, reception, interaction) up to the C1/B2.2 level of the Council of Europe (L-LIN/12).
Capacity for learning As specific objectives, instrumental to the previous ones, communication sciences graduates will have fully mastered the:
- skills related to the main practices and research methods of each discipline. Graduates must be able to exercise the ability to quickly search for and obtain all necessary data and information to deepen their knowledge of the various communication and cultural processes occurring in society, both in their theoretical formulations and regarding their implications in different contexts and themes; they must therefore have also acquired skills and abilities in identifying and retrieving sources from which to extract the aforementioned information, both national and international in origin; they must also possess the ability to select the most effective research practices and methodologies for analyzing and deepening specific research topics and/or questions, with reference to the most recent trends in the various sectors of communication sciences; Graduates must finally demonstrate the ability to operate in an interdisciplinary perspective.
To be able to undertake subsequent studies with a high degree of autonomy, graduates must:
- develop the ability to learn both the content and the scientific terminology that identifies each disciplinary field or research area covered by the educational offer;
- learn to use synergistically the different sources through which educational content is delivered (lectures, seminars, study texts, handouts, etc.);
- learn to focus on their specific knowledge interests and select didactic and training activities according to these (referring both to course selection, where this option is available, and to the selection of topics they wish to deepen within each course and for the purpose of writing the thesis).

Judgment Autonomy Graduates will have acquired those project and operational skills that enable them to critically analyze and professionally manage various communication processes within different contexts and institutions, as well as evaluate the effectiveness of their operation in diverse operational sectors (economic, legislative, technological, social).

They must also be able to demonstrate having acquired the ability and confidence to manage complex processes, both by identifying their operational purposes and by resolving issues related to the appropriate choice of communication forms required by the needs of specific professional fields.

SECTION: Communication Skills
URL: https://unisi.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/10692

Communication Skills.
Through participation in frontal lectures, written and oral exercises, laboratories using technical equipment, guided visits to external realities, and specific projects developed during courses, graduates will possess the necessary skills for socializing information and sectoral knowledge acquired during their studies, as well as for presenting and valorizing results (creative, analytical, project-based) achieved; whether in written or oral presentations, graduates must demonstrate the ability to operate in different communication situations, varying registers and codes in relation to interlocutors and the purpose of the communication process; they must also demonstrate the ability to use graphic, media, and computer supports; in the case of technologically mediated communication, graduates must be able to select the most suitable means to reach a specific audience and show the ability to adapt content and communication forms to the technological and cultural characteristics of the medium in question. In addition to acquiring skills related to the communication/presentation/dissemination of information, problems, and ideas in an individual form, graduates must develop the ability to organize and manage complex communication processes involving multiple subjects. Graduates will have developed their communication skills through: theoretical knowledge acquired through frontal lectures, oral and/or written exposition necessary for passing examination assessments, intermediate exercises, seminar and workshop activities. In each of these settings, continuous interaction with professors and fellow students occurs. The final thesis corresponds to the ability to communicate all phases of a project, from its conception to final use, using available documentation and scientific literature, with language accessible to both professionals and a broader audience. This ability is refined throughout the training path through all verification tests, passing exams, and written and oral assessment exercises; reports and elaborations from seminar and workshop activities. The acquisition of advanced communication skills in English will enable graduates to transmit competencies and information, identify and solve problems in English. In this perspective, the possibility of teaching some curricular disciplines in English is provided.
Employment and professional opportunities for graduates.
Advertising Technician
(1) Advertising agencies
(2) Companies, organizations, consulting firms dealing with tourism promotion
(3) Communication offices of companies and organizations
(4) External relations offices, URP of public administrations
(5) Media centers, companies operating in mass communications with their own advertising collection (television, radio, web providers, web publications, commercial blogs)
Public Relations Officer
(1) Companies and consulting firms dealing with public relations and event organization
(2) Communication and/or public relations offices of companies or organizations
(3) External relations offices, URP of public administrations Advertising Technician
(1) Basic knowledge of marketing, mass communication, and market analysis.
(2) Semiotic analysis skills of texts, ability to analyze stories, meanings, and values associated with a brand and/or product;
(3) Skills in analyzing advertising campaigns and knowledge in the field of media and new media.
The training offered in advertising and mass communication is combined with a solid general humanistic culture, good knowledge of the English language, and adequate knowledge in communication and organizational contexts (competencies in communication psychology, persuasion techniques, and interpersonal communication techniques)
Public Relations Officer
(1) Basic competencies in corporate communication and analysis of communication and information campaigns by different subjects (companies, organizations, institutions, etc.); competencies in communication psychology, persuasion techniques, and interpersonal communication techniques
(2) Competencies in the fields of media, new media, mass communication, corporate communication, and advertising.
The training offered in public relations and mass communication is combined with a solid general humanistic culture, good knowledge of the English language, and adequate knowledge in communication and organizational contexts Advertising Technician General marketing and corporate communication competencies;
(2) Competencies in communication psychology, persuasion techniques, and interpersonal communication techniques;
(3) Semiotic text analysis skills and problem-solving abilities.
Function in work context.
Advertising Technician The advertising technician assists specialists:
(1) in promoting the market activities of a company or organization;
(2) in creating a positive image for the company or organization.
Additionally,
(3) applies and follows procedures to plan and activate various types of promotions and advertising campaigns on different media.
Public Relations Officer The public relations officer assists specialists:
(1) in seeking, selecting, collecting, and organizing favorable information and/or advertising material for the company or organization;
(2) in organizing and sponsoring events of particular importance and visibility for the company or organization, not directly related to advertising promotion.
Advertising Technician The advertising technician assists specialists:
(1) in developing marketing strategies for the company or organization;
(2) in controlling the efficiency of the marketing strategy and monitoring uptake.
Additionally,
(3) applies procedures set by the company or organization to collect information on the target public and communication strategies, analyze, organize, and present them in a relevant and meaningful way to specialists and sector managers.
Additional information.
https://www.dispoc.unisi.it/it https://www.unisi.it Specific educational objectives description.
Cultural and creative industries occupy an increasingly central role in the economies of contemporary societies, but the contribution these industries make to social, economic, and cultural well-being varies from country to country and depends on political, cultural, social, and economic factors. Understanding these dynamics and studying the main historical, political, and social disciplines alongside linguistic, cognitive, and semiotic theories allows navigating this new complexity with appropriate analytical tools.
Graduates in Communication Sciences acquire a set of competencies and skills derived from human and social sciences. The dual objective is a) a deeper understanding of the present time in its historical, social, psychological, and anthropological aspects beyond the Western world, and b) up-to-date knowledge of linguistic, semiotic, and technological communication methods. These competencies form the common core of first and second-year teachings.
In particular, human and social sciences (M-STO/04, SPS/04, SPS/07, SPS/08, M-DEA/01, M-PSI/01, SECS-S/01) are represented by mandatory teachings in contemporary history, studying the evolution of globalization, and sociology teachings studying cultural and communication processes.
The study course places particular emphasis on social research methodology, also through cognitive psychology, which provides basic knowledge for understanding cognitive processes and develops competencies related to psychological and social research methodologies; and public opinion science to familiarize students with major empirical research on the nature of public opinion and the interaction between public opinion and public policies; additionally, students may choose a statistics teaching. Teachings regarding visual sociology, the relationship between journalism and new media are available; further anthropological aspects are present through the possibility of choosing teachings in cultural anthropology or consumption anthropology.
An introduction to applied informatics provides students with a foundation of knowledge to familiarize them with the terminology and concepts of the computer world and offers the basic elements to use all hardware and software tools useful for supporting their teaching and learning activities.
For communication disciplines (L-LIN/01, L-LIN/12, L-FIL-LET/12, M-FIL/05, ING-INF/05, L-ART/06), first and second-year teachings offer semiotics teachings for fundamental competencies related to semiotics as a general theory of communication and to provide basic tools for semiotic text analysis. Theoretical understanding of linguistic description is introduced through general linguistics, the relationship between society and language through sociolinguistics, and the study of the relationship between mass media, digital culture, and society; communication skills in good Italian are developed, along with the ability to create appropriate texts through a writing laboratory for creative and cultural industries; other languages become objects of study with an English media language and language examination. Students may choose teachings on film language theories and techniques or communication law, journalism history.
In the third year, common teachings provide further specialized knowledge on interaction design (M-PSI/01), offering a methodological framework for the ideation and design process of interactive artifacts; knowledge of rhetoric and persuasive languages (M-FIL/05) and experimental economics (SECS-P/01).
Optional teachings can be chosen in 4 different areas corresponding to 4 professional opportunities: Linguistic-Cognitive Disciplines; Technology and Communication; Communication and Market; Political Communication.
In the first area, teachings include philosophy and cognition (M-FIL/01), further linguistic knowledge through the study of Italian Sign Language (L-LIN/01), or applied linguistics (L-LIN/01). In the second area concerning communication and market, students may choose teachings on marketing (SECS-P/08), advertising, communication, and consumption (SPS/08), or a data visualization laboratory (GGR/02). In the third area, teachings concern multimodal aspects of technology and communication such as video and graphic production (ING-INF/05), the relationship between perception and graphic communication (M-PSI/01), and human-machine interaction for developing theoretical, methodological, and practical competencies in designing interaction between humans and technological and non-technological artifacts, and usability, experience, and adequacy criteria of interaction, along with the theoretical and methodological foundations of the human-centered design approach (ICAR/13). In the fourth area, teachings concern the language of political regimes (SPS/03) and political communication (SPS/04). Additionally, students have 12 credits to choose according to their interests.
The mandatory English language teaching aims for an advanced level of communication competence (C1/B2.2 of the Council of Europe Reference Framework). The course includes acquiring credits through internships and pre-graduation traineeships, training experiences, and professionalizing activities at a structure conventioned with the University, offering students the opportunity to directly experience the world of work and develop knowledge acquired during their academic training. Additional credits are dedicated to further knowledge useful for entering the world of work. The Erasmus+ Programme allows students to spend a period of study ranging from 3 to 12 months at a European university in the disciplinary area of interest. The conclusion of the training path involves a final assessment consisting of an independently produced elaboration by the student to verify and evaluate competencies in source retrieval, methodological skills, mastery of scientific literature, critical abilities, and independent judgment. The final assessment may be an elaboration/thesis or another mode according to the methodology most suitable for the chosen discipline.
The expansion of the knowledge economy and communication and information technologies requires researchers and professionals prepared to interpret their risks and opportunities. Overall, the study course prepares students to enter the world of communication professions.
The course also prepares students to continue their studies to specialize at the University of Siena with master's degrees in Communication Strategies and Techniques, International Studies, Language and Mind: Linguistics and Cognitive Studies, Anthropology and Languages of Image, or the first-level master's degree in Corporate Communication. Languages, Tools, Technologies.
